Clinical Reference

Antibiotics

On this page
Antibiotics are chosen by answering four questions in order: what organ is infected → what bugs live there → what does the patient's exposure history force me to cover → how sick are they right now. Everything else — the generation, the spectrum, the route — falls out of those four answers.
Empiric = broad, definitive = narrow 48–72 h antibiotic time-out Cultures BEFORE the first dose Septic shock → antibiotics within 1 h No cephalosporin covers Enterococcus, Listeria or atypicals

How antibiotics work

🧬

Five targets — every antibiotic you will ever prescribe hits one of them

A bacterium is a pressurised bag. Inside, osmotic pressure runs several atmospheres above the outside world; the only thing preventing the cell from bursting is a rigid mesh of cross-linked sugar–peptide polymer called peptidoglycan. Human cells have no peptidoglycan, no bacterial ribosome, and no bacterial folate-synthesis pathway — and that difference is the entire basis of selective toxicity. Every antibiotic class is an attack on a structure the bacterium has and we do not.

There are only five places to attack, and knowing which one a drug hits tells you almost everything else about it — whether it kills or merely stalls, whether it works inside a cell, whether it penetrates the CSF, and what it will do to your patient's kidneys, marrow, or QT interval.

a walled city under siege. β-lactams and vancomycin stop the masons repairing the wall, so the wall fails under its own internal pressure. Daptomycin and polymyxins punch holes in the gate itself. Aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, macrolides, clindamycin and linezolid silence the city's factories (ribosomes) so nothing gets rebuilt. Fluoroquinolones and metronidazole shred the blueprints (DNA). TMP-SMX starves the city by cutting off the supply of raw material (folate → thymidine) it needs to copy those blueprints. Cutting the water supply (bacteriostatic) is enough when the defenders are healthy; when the immune system is absent — neutropenia, endocarditis vegetations, meningitis, prosthetic material — you must burn the city down (bactericidal).

The five druggable targets. Locate a drug on this map and you can predict its behaviour: wall-active agents need actively dividing bacteria, ribosome agents get into cells (atypicals), and only lipophilic small molecules cross an uninflamed blood–brain barrier.
Peptidoglycan. Alternating NAG–NAM sugar strands cross-linked by short peptides ending in D-Ala-D-Ala. That terminal D-Ala-D-Ala is the bullseye: β-lactams mimic it, vancomycin binds it.
Image: Peptidoglycan-simple.png — Bradleyhintze, CC0 (Wikimedia Commons)
The transpeptidase (PBP) reaction that β-lactams block — the cross-link that converts a loose mesh into a pressure vessel. Block it and the cell lyses.
Image: Simple transpeptidase machanism cartoon.png — Bradleyhintze, CC0 (Wikimedia Commons)
The β-lactam ring — the strained four-membered amide ring shared by penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems and aztreonam. Its ring strain is what makes it reactive enough to acylate the PBP active site, and also what makes it a target for β-lactamases.
Image: Chemical Structure of Penicillin.png — SM Smith96, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
Where β-lactamase cuts. The enzyme hydrolyses the same ring, opening it and destroying the D-Ala-D-Ala mimicry. β-lactamase inhibitors (clavulanate, tazobactam, avibactam) are decoys that occupy this enzyme instead.
Image: Site of cleavage by beta-lactamase.jpg — UIC College of Pharmacy, Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
The class map in one figure — cell-wall, membrane, protein-synthesis, nucleic-acid and folate-pathway agents side by side. Every drug in this guide belongs to one of these columns.
Image: How do different antibiotics work?.png — Our World in Data - Saloni Dattani (adapted from Sanseverino et al. 2018; Hutchings, Truman and Wilkinson 2019; icons from NIH BioArt), CC BY 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
Cidal vs static matters in exactly four situations. For most infections in an immunocompetent host, a bacteriostatic drug plus a working immune system cures the patient just as well. But when the host cannot finish the job you must kill: (1) endocarditis — bacteria sit in an avascular fibrin vegetation neutrophils cannot enter; (2) meningitis — the CSF is a relatively immunoprivileged, opsonin-poor space; (3) profound neutropenia (ANC <500); (4) osteomyelitis / prosthetic material biofilm. In those settings pick a bactericidal agent and dose it aggressively.

Bactericidal vs bacteriostatic — the working list

Bactericidal (kills)Bacteriostatic (stalls)The nuance
β-lactams (all)Macrolidesβ-lactams are time-dependent killers — efficacy tracks the fraction of the dosing interval free drug stays above the MIC (%fT>MIC). That is why you shorten the interval or extend the infusion rather than raise the peak.
Vancomycin, lipoglycopeptidesClindamycinVancomycin is technically cidal but kills slowly; it is inferior to an antistaphylococcal β-lactam for MSSA bacteraemia and should never be used when the isolate is MSSA.
AminoglycosidesTetracyclines / tigecyclineAminoglycosides are concentration-dependent with a long post-antibiotic effect — hence once-daily extended-interval dosing (higher peak, longer trough-free window, less toxicity).
FluoroquinolonesLinezolidFluoroquinolones are concentration-dependent (AUC/MIC driven). Linezolid is static against staph/enterococci but cidal against streptococci.
MetronidazoleTMP-SMX (static alone, cidal in combination)Metronidazole is a prodrug reduced only in a low-redox (anaerobic) environment — which is exactly why it has no aerobic activity whatsoever.
Daptomycin, polymyxinsChloramphenicolDaptomycin is rapidly cidal and concentration-dependent — but is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant and therefore can never be used for pneumonia.
The single most useful PK/PD fact on the wards: β-lactams are time-dependent. If a patient with severe sepsis is failing pip-tazo, the answer is usually extended-infusion dosing (4.5 g over 4 hours q8h) rather than a bigger single dose. Conversely, if a patient is failing an aminoglycoside, the peak was too low — give a bigger dose, less often.
🛡️

How bacteria fight back — the four resistance mechanisms

Resistance is not something antibiotics create; it is something they select for. Every course of antibiotics kills the susceptible flora and leaves the resistant survivors with an empty niche to repopulate. That is the entire biological argument for stewardship, and it is why the correct answer to "should I broaden?" is so often "no — I should narrow."

Gram-negatives have an extra outer membrane, which is why they can combine mechanisms 1, 3 and 4 and become pan-resistant — and why gram-negative resistance is the harder clinical problem.
Why gram-negatives are harder. A gram-positive organism has a thick but naked peptidoglycan wall — the drug only has to get through the mesh. A gram-negative has a thin wall wrapped in an outer lipopolysaccharide membrane whose only doors are porin channels, plus a periplasmic space where β-lactamases sit concentrated exactly where the drug must pass, plus efflux pumps. Vancomycin fails against gram-negatives for a purely mechanical reason: the molecule is too large to fit through the porins.

The spectrum grid

🗺️

Antibiotic × organism — the single most useful table in this guide

Learn this grid and empiric therapy becomes arithmetic. You pick the syndrome, you list the organisms you must not miss, and then you choose the smallest box on this grid that contains all of them. Everything wider than that box is collateral damage: C. difficile, resistance selection, and a patient who gets an antibiotic allergy label they will carry for forty years.

The caveats that turn a "✓" into a treatment failure

  • Ertapenem has no antipseudomonal activity and no enterococcal activity. It is the once-daily, outpatient-friendly carbapenem for ESBL infections — never the carbapenem for the septic ICU patient.
  • Ceftriaxone's anaerobic "~" means oral anaerobes only. It does not cover B. fragilis, which is why intra-abdominal regimens built on ceftriaxone must add metronidazole.
  • Piperacillin-tazobactam's ESBL "~" is a real clinical failure. The MERINO trial randomised ESBL bloodstream infection to pip-tazo vs meropenem and found higher 30-day mortality with pip-tazo (12.3% vs 3.7%) — it did not meet non-inferiority. Treat proven ESBL bacteraemia with a carbapenem.
  • Daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant. Every column above is true except in the lung, where it does not work at all.
  • Vancomycin's enterococcal "✓" excludes VRE (vanA/vanB alter the D-Ala-D-Ala target to D-Ala-D-Lac). For VRE use linezolid or daptomycin (high dose).
  • Cefepime's ESBL "✗" is because ESBLs hydrolyse it despite in-vitro susceptibility at low inocula; cefepime is the right answer for AmpC organisms (Enterobacter, Serratia, Citrobacter), where ceftriaxone will select for resistance mid-treatment.
  • Tigecycline covers everything and is right for almost nothing systemic — it achieves very low serum concentrations, carries an FDA boxed warning for increased all-cause mortality, and must not be used for bacteraemia, pneumonia, or urinary infection.
  • Nitrofurantoin only works in urine. It concentrates in bladder urine and achieves no meaningful tissue or serum levels — so it is right for cystitis and wrong for pyelonephritis, prostatitis, or any bacteraemia.
  • Ciprofloxacin is not a strep drug. Using it for cellulitis or pneumonia is a classic error; if you need a quinolone for a respiratory pathogen, you need levofloxacin or moxifloxacin.
  • Moxifloxacin does not achieve therapeutic urine concentrations and is not antipseudomonal — never use it for UTI.
The three "holes" worth memorising cold. Ask of any regimen: does it cover MRSA? does it cover Pseudomonas? does it cover anaerobes? Almost every empiric-therapy question in medicine reduces to plugging one of those three holes. Ceftriaxone has all three holes. Cefepime plugs Pseudomonas only. Pip-tazo plugs Pseudomonas and anaerobes. Nothing but vancomycin/linezolid/daptomycin/ceftaroline plugs MRSA.

Cephalosporin generations

🪜

The staircase — how coverage shifts from gram-positive to gram-negative and back

The generations are not a ranking of "strength." They are a description of a trade: as you climb from 1st to 4th generation the molecule gains gram-negative reach — better outer-membrane penetration and increasing stability against gram-negative β-lactamases — and, until the 4th generation, gradually gives up gram-positive potency. The 5th generation breaks the pattern by adding the one thing no other β-lactam has: activity against MRSA's altered PBP2a.

Gram-positive potency dips through the 3rd generation and recovers at the 4th and 5th; gram-negative reach climbs to a peak at the 4th generation. The gaps at the bottom never close.
GenAgents (IV · PO)What it addsWhat it loses / never hadWhere you actually use it
1stIV cefazolin · PO cephalexin, cefadroxilExcellent MSSA and streptococcal killing — cefazolin is the best MSSA drug alongside nafcillin. Narrow gram-negative: P·E·cK — Proteus mirabilis, E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae.No H. influenzae, no Pseudomonas, no anaerobes below the diaphragm, no CNS penetration.Surgical prophylaxis, cellulitis, MSSA bacteraemia and endocarditis, uncomplicated cystitis, IV→PO step-down to cephalexin.
2ndIV cefuroxime, cefoxitin, cefotetan · PO cefuroxime axetil, cefaclor, cefprozilHENS-PEcK — adds H. influenzae, Enterobacter, Neisseria, Serratia. The cephamycins (cefoxitin, cefotetan) uniquely add B. fragilis anaerobic coverage.Loses some gram-positive potency vs 1st gen. Still no Pseudomonas, no reliable CNS penetration. Cefotetan carries an NMTT side chain → hypoprothrombinaemia and a disulfiram-like reaction.Cefuroxime: outpatient respiratory/sinus. Cefoxitin/cefotetan: colorectal and gynaecologic surgical prophylaxis, mild community-acquired intra-abdominal infection.
3rdIV ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, ceftazidime · PO cefpodoxime, cefdinir, cefiximeBroad Enterobacterales coverage and — for ceftriaxone/cefotaxime — reliable CSF penetration. Ceftriaxone needs no renal adjustment (biliary excretion). Ceftazidime is the outlier: it trades gram-positive activity for Pseudomonas.No Pseudomonas (except ceftazidime). No B. fragilis. Ceftriaxone drives AmpC de-repression in Enterobacter/Serratia/Citrobacter. Ceftriaxone causes biliary sludging and is contraindicated in neonates with calcium-containing IV fluids.Ceftriaxone is the workhorse: CAP, pyelonephritis, meningitis (2 g q12h), gonorrhoea, SBP, cellulitis with gram-negative risk. Ceftazidime: pseudomonal infection when you want to spare gram-positive flora.
4thIV cefepimeZwitterion — penetrates the gram-negative outer membrane fast and has low affinity for AmpC β-lactamases. Covers Pseudomonas and regains 1st-generation-level gram-positive activity. Penetrates CSF.Not stable to ESBLs. No B. fragilis, no enterococcus, no MRSA. Cefepime neurotoxicity (encephalopathy, myoclonus, non-convulsive status) in renal impairment when the dose is not adjusted.Febrile neutropenia monotherapy, HAP/VAP, nosocomial sepsis, AmpC organisms, healthcare-associated meningitis.
5thIV ceftaroline (ceftobiprole where available)The only β-lactam that binds PBP2a → covers MRSA, plus penicillin-nonsusceptible pneumococcus and E. faecalis.No Pseudomonas, no E. faecium/VRE, no ESBL. Can cause neutropenia with prolonged use.MRSA SSTI and CAP; salvage for MRSA bacteraemia failing vancomycin (often combined with daptomycin).
a camera lens. The 1st generation is a portrait lens — beautifully sharp on one subject (gram-positive cocci), no peripheral vision. Each generation zooms out, taking in more of the gram-negative landscape but softening the centre. The 4th generation is the wide-angle that somehow keeps the centre sharp. The 5th generation is a specialty lens built to photograph exactly one thing nobody else can: MRSA.

Mnemonics that actually survive call

MnemonicExpansionWhat it locks in
1st gen: "PEcK"Proteus mirabilis · E. coli · Klebsiella pneumoniaeThe entire gram-negative reach of cefazolin/cephalexin. If the organism is not one of these three, a 1st generation will not cover it.
2nd gen: "HENS-PEcK"H. influenzae · Enterobacter · Neisseria · Serratia — plus the 1st-gen PEcKThe 2nd generation is the 1st generation "pecked at by hens" — same core, four more gram-negatives.
Cephamycins: "FOX and TAN fight the anaerobes"Cefoxitin and cefotetan are the only cephalosporins with real B. fragilis activityStops you from adding metronidazole unnecessarily to cefoxitin — and reminds you every other cephalosporin needs metronidazole for an intra-abdominal source.
The gaps: "LAME"Listeria · Atypicals (Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydia) · MRSA · EnterococcusWhat no cephalosporin covers (except ceftaroline for the M). This is why meningitis in a patient ≥50 needs ampicillin added, and why CAP needs a macrolide or doxycycline alongside ceftriaxone.
Antipseudomonal cephs: "the TAZ and the PIME"Ceftazidime · cefepime · ceftolozane-tazobactamThe only three cephalosporins you can hang for Pseudomonas. Ceftriaxone never covers Pseudomonas — a very common and very dangerous assumption.
Two cephalosporin errors that harm patients: (1) using ceftriaxone for an Enterobacter, Serratia or Citrobacter isolate — even when the lab reports it susceptible, inducible AmpC β-lactamase emerges on treatment and the patient relapses with a resistant organism; use cefepime or a carbapenem. (2) using cefazolin for a CNS infection — it does not cross the blood–brain barrier at any dose.

The classes — dose, mechanism, monitoring

💊

Every agent you will order, with its adult dose in normal renal function

Mechanism. All β-lactams are structural mimics of the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of the peptidoglycan pentapeptide. They acylate the active site of the penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) that cross-link the wall, so the cell keeps making new peptidoglycan strands but can no longer stitch them together. Autolysins continue chewing the old wall, the mesh fails, and the cell lyses under its own osmotic pressure. This only works on actively dividing bacteria — which is why β-lactams are useless against dormant organisms and why they are time-dependent killers.

β-lactam efficacy is driven by %fT>MIC — the percentage of the dosing interval that free drug stays above the MIC (roughly 40–50% for penicillins/carbapenems, 60–70% for cephalosporins, and higher in critical illness). Raising a single dose barely helps; shortening the interval or extending the infusion is what fixes an under-treated β-lactam.

Penicillins

DrugIV dosePO doseWhy / spectrum nicheToxicity & monitoring
Penicillin G (aqueous)2–4 million units q4h (18–24 MU/day)—Drug of choice for S. pyogenes, syphilis, susceptible viridans strep endocarditis, Clostridium, actinomyces. Nothing has ever beaten it for Group A strep — zero documented penicillin resistance.Hypersensitivity; seizures at very high doses in renal failure (penicillin G is a GABA-A antagonist); the potassium salt carries a substantial potassium load, so watch K⁺ at 18–24 MU/day. Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction in syphilis.
Penicillin G benzathine1.2 MU IM ×1 (pharyngitis); 2.4 MU IM ×1 (early syphilis, weekly ×3 for late latent)—Depot IM formulation giving weeks of low-level exposure — the only regimen proven for syphilis.Never give IV — cardiorespiratory arrest. Injection-site pain.

The MRSA problem. Methicillin resistance is not a β-lactamase — it is the mecA gene encoding an alternative transpeptidase, PBP2a, whose active site has such low affinity for β-lactams that the cell keeps building its wall while every penicillin and cephalosporin is present. That is why adding a β-lactamase inhibitor does nothing, and why only four kinds of drug work: glycopeptides, the lipopeptide, the oxazolidinones, and the one cephalosporin engineered to fit PBP2a.

Never treat MSSA with vancomycin. Multiple cohorts show higher failure and mortality in MSSA bacteraemia treated with vancomycin compared with cefazolin or an antistaphylococcal penicillin. Aminoglycosides

Aminoglycosides bind irreversibly to the 30S subunit, causing mRNA misreading and membrane damage — one of the few bactericidal protein-synthesis inhibitors. Uptake across the bacterial membrane is oxygen-dependent, which explains three clinical facts at once: no anaerobic activity, poor activity in the acidic hypoxic environment of an abscess, and poor activity in lung tissue.

DrugExtended-interval doseTraditional / synergy doseTargetsMonitoring
Gentamicin5–7 mg/kg q24h (adjusted body weight if obese)1–1.7 mg/kg q8h; synergy dosing 3 mg/kg/day divided q8h for enterococcal or streptococcal endocarditisGram-negative aerobes; synergy with a cell-wall agent against enterococci, staph and viridans strep.Peak 5–10 (traditional) / trough <1–2 mg/L; synergy peak ~3–4, trough <1. Creatinine every 2–3 days, daily in the unstable. Audiometry if >7–10 days.
Tobramycin5–7 mg/kg q24h1–1.7 mg/kg q8hSlightly more potent than gentamicin against Pseudomonas — the preferred aminoglycoside for pseudomonal pneumonia and cystic fibrosis.Same as gentamicin.
Amikacin15–20 mg/kg q24h7.5 mg/kg q12hMost resistant to aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes — retains activity against many MDR gram-negatives, ESBL and CRE, plus atypical mycobacteria.Peak 25–40, trough <5–8 mg/L. Same nephro/ototoxicity monitoring.
Why once-daily beats three-times-daily. Aminoglycoside killing is concentration-dependent (peak/MIC ≥8–10), and they have a long post-antibiotic effect, so a big peak works better. Toxicity, by contrast, is saturable uptake into renal tubular and cochlear hair cells — which means it depends on how long the concentration stays high, not how high it gets. One large daily dose therefore maximises efficacy and minimises toxicity simultaneously. The exception is synergy dosing in endocarditis, where you want continuous low-level exposure alongside a cell-wall agent and use small divided doses.
Aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity is typically non-oliguric and appears after 5–7 days; ototoxicity is often irreversible and may be vestibular (oscillopsia, gait instability) rather than auditory. Avoid concomitant vancomycin, loop diuretics, contrast, NSAIDs and amphotericin where possible, and stop as soon as culture data allow.

Coverage by pathogen

🦠

Read it backwards — "the culture grew X, now what?"

The spectrum grid answers "what does this drug cover?" This table answers the question you actually get paged about: "the blood cultures are growing X — is my patient on the right antibiotic?" The drug of choice is listed first; resistance figures are US national estimates and will differ from your hospital's antibiogram, which always wins.

Gram-positive cocci in clusters — Staphylococcus. Clusters mean staph; your next decision is MSSA vs MRSA and whether this is a contaminant (coagulase-negative in 1 of 4 bottles) or the real thing.
Image: Gram positive cocci in clusters.jpg — Microrao, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci — Streptococcus pneumoniae. Pairs and chains mean strep; in a CAP sputum or CSF this is your answer.
Image: Gram stain of Streptococcus pneumoniae.jpg — Arnold Kaufman, CC0 (Wikimedia Commons)
Gram-negative rods — E. coli and the rest of the Enterobacterales. In a septic patient this is the finding that makes you ask: does this patient need Pseudomonas or ESBL coverage?
Image: E choli Gram.JPG — Bobjgalindo, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

Haemolysis on blood agar. Complete (β) haemolysis clears the agar — S. pyogenes, S. agalactiae. Partial (α) haemolysis leaves a green halo — pneumococcus and viridans strep.

the AmpC organisms (IDSA 2024)		Cefepime 2 g IV q8h or a carbapenem. Non-β-lactam options: TMP-SMX, fluoroquinolone by susceptibility.Ceftriaxone and other 3rd-generation cephalosporins — even when reported susceptible. Also all penicillins and 1st/2nd-generation cephalosporins.These carry an inducible chromosomal AmpC β-lactamase. Exposure to a 3rd-generation cephalosporin selects de-repressed mutants and the patient relapses mid-course with a resistant organism. Cefepime is stable because it is a poor AmpC substrate and penetrates fast. IDSA 2024 narrowed the list to the three organisms at high enough risk of clinically significant AmpC production to matter: Enterobacter cloacae complex, Klebsiella aerogenes and Citrobacter freundii. The older mnemonics "SPICE" and "HECK-Yes" are still widely taught but are obsolete and over-inclusive — "indole-positive Proteus" in particular is now considered wrong. Learn the three organisms rather than the mnemonic.
Pseudomonas aeruginosaCefepime 2 g q8h · pip-tazo 4.5 g q6h (or extended infusion) · meropenem 1–2 g q8h · ceftazidime 2 g q8h · ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q8h / 750 mg PO BID (the only reliable oral option) · aztreonam in severe β-lactam allergy. MDR: ceftolozane-tazobactam, ceftazidime-avibactam, cefiderocol.Ceftriaxone, ertapenem, ampicillin-sulbactam, moxifloxacin — all commonly assumed to cover Pseudomonas and none of them do. Also all oral cephalosporins.Risk factors that should make you cover it empirically: structural lung disease (bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, advanced COPD on steroids), neutropenia, recent broad-spectrum antibiotics or hospitalisation, prior Pseudomonas isolation, burns, ventilator, indwelling devices. Combines all four resistance mechanisms — it can become resistant during therapy, so re-culture if the patient is not improving.
ESBL producers
usually CTX-M in E. coli/Klebsiella		A carbapenem — meropenem 1 g q8h for severe infection, ertapenem 1 g q24h for stable patients and OPAT. Non-bacteraemic cystitis: nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin, or an aminoglycoside.Piperacillin-tazobactam for bloodstream infection (the MERINO trial found 30-day mortality 12.3% with pip-tazo vs 3.7% with meropenem and failed non-inferiority). Cefepime is also unreliable. All 3rd-generation cephalosporins.ESBLs hydrolyse penicillins, all cephalosporins and aztreonam, but not carbapenems or cephamycins. Risk factors: prior ESBL, recent β-lactam or fluoroquinolone exposure, healthcare exposure, travel to high-prevalence regions, long-term care residence.
CRE
carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales		KPC (class A): ceftazidime-avibactam 2.5 g q8h or meropenem-vaborbactam 4 g q8h. Metallo-β-lactamase (NDM/VIM/IMP): cefiderocol, or ceftazidime-avibactam plus aztreonam. OXA-48: ceftazidime-avibactam.Ceftazidime-avibactam and meropenem-vaborbactam against metallo-β-lactamases — a common and lethal mistake. Ertapenem. Tigecycline for bacteraemia.Always identify the carbapenemase — the mechanism dictates the drug, and the epidemiology is shifting fast. In CDC Emerging Infections Program surveillance, NDM rose from 5.4% of carbapenemase-producing CRE in 2016 to 39.8% in 2023, while KPC fell from 92.8% to 53.0%. Since avibactam and vaborbactam do not touch metallo-β-lactamases, "CRE → give ceftazidime-avibactam" is no longer a safe reflex. Involve ID early. Colistin is a last resort with real nephrotoxicity.
Acinetobacter baumanniiAmpicillin-sulbactam (high dose — sulbactam has intrinsic activity) or a carbapenem; MDR: cefiderocol, high-dose sulbactam-durlobactam, polymyxins, minocycline.Ertapenem, aztreonam, ceftriaxone.Almost always ICU-acquired, often ventilator-associated; frequently colonisation rather than infection — treat the patient, not the sputum.
Stenotrophomonas maltophiliaTMP-SMX (15 mg/kg/day of TMP divided) is the drug of choice. Alternatives: levofloxacin, minocycline, ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam.All carbapenems — intrinsically resistant (it makes a metallo-β-lactamase). Most β-lactams.Classically emerges because the patient has been on a carbapenem. A gram-negative rod appearing on day 10 of meropenem is Stenotrophomonas until proven otherwise.
Haemophilus influenzaeAmoxicillin-clavulanate, 2nd/3rd-generation cephalosporin, azithromycin, doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone.Plain amoxicillin/ampicillin in β-lactamase-producing strains (roughly a quarter to a third of isolates).A key CAP and COPD-exacerbation pathogen, especially in smokers. Non-typeable strains are not prevented by the Hib vaccine.
Moraxella catarrhalisAmox-clav, cefuroxime, azithromycin, doxycycline, TMP-SMX.Plain amoxicillin — nearly all isolates produce β-lactamase.Sinusitis, otitis, COPD exacerbation.
Neisseria meningitidisCeftriaxone 2 g IV q12h (or penicillin G 4 MU q4h if susceptible) ×7 days. Prophylaxis for close contacts: ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO ×1, rifampin 600 mg BID ×2 d, or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM ×1.Vancomycin.Droplet precautions for 24 h. Check terminal complement (C5–C9) function in recurrent or unusual serogroup disease, and in anyone on eculizumab/ravulizumab.
Neisseria gonorrhoeaeCeftriaxone 500 mg IM ×1 (1 g if ≥150 kg); treat for chlamydia with doxycycline 100 mg BID ×7 d unless excluded.Fluoroquinolones (widespread resistance — no longer recommended), oral cefixime (second-line only), azithromycin monotherapy.Resistance is escalating globally; CDC now recommends ceftriaxone monotherapy at the higher dose rather than the old dual-therapy approach.

Oral / above-diaphragm anaerobes

🔬

Reading the micro lab — susceptibility, MIC, and what "S" actually means

The susceptibility report is not a ranking of drug strength. S / I / R are site- and dose-specific predictions made by comparing the organism's MIC to a breakpoint that assumes a particular drug, dose and body site. A pneumococcus reported "penicillin-susceptible" for a lung infection may be "penicillin-resistant" by CSF breakpoints for the same MIC — the bug did not change; the achievable concentration at the site did.

Disk diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) — a susceptible isolate. Antibiotic diffuses out of each paper disk into the agar; a wide clear zone means growth was inhibited at achievable concentrations.
Image: Antibiotic suceptible bacteria.jpg — Microrao, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
The same test, a multidrug-resistant isolate. Bacteria grow right up to the disks — no zone, no activity. This is what an ESBL or MDR Pseudomonas looks like on a plate.
Image: Antibiotic resistant bacteria.jpg — Microrao, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
Gradient strip (Etest) — reading an MIC. The strip carries a continuous antibiotic gradient; you read the MIC where the elliptical growth margin intersects the scale. This is how a vancomycin or oxacillin MIC gets onto your patient's chart.
Image: Etest Vancomycin S aureus.jpg — Microrao, JJMMC, Davangere, Karnataka, India, Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
The same technique, whole-plate view — S. pneumoniae tested against cefotaxime. The teardrop of inhibited growth narrows toward the strip; where its edge meets the scale is the MIC that the lab compares against the breakpoint.
Image: Streptococcus pneumoniae tested with Cefotaxime.jpg — Nathan Reading (Flickr), CC BY 2.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
ESBL confirmation. Ceftazidime alone versus ceftazidime + clavulanate: a ≥5 mm zone expansion when the inhibitor is added proves the resistance is β-lactamase-mediated. This is the test behind the word "ESBL" on your report.
Image: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase.jpg — Microrao, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
What the report saysWhat it actually meansWhat you do
MIC (minimum inhibitory concentration)The lowest drug concentration that stops visible growth in vitro. It is a property of the organism–drug pair, not a measure of how good the drug is.Never compare MICs between different drugs — a vancomycin MIC of 1 and a cefazolin MIC of 1 mean completely different things. Compare only against that drug's breakpoint.
S — susceptibleStandard dosing should achieve concentrations at the infection site that exceed the MIC for long enough to work.Use it — and prefer the narrowest S agent on the panel.
I — intermediate / "susceptible-dose-dependent"Achievable only with maximal dosing or where the drug concentrates (urine, bile).Use only at maximum dose and only if the site concentrates the drug; otherwise choose another agent.
R — resistantPredicted failure at any safe dose.Do not use, regardless of how well the patient seems to be doing.
Suppressed / not reportedLabs deliberately hide broad-spectrum results (cascade reporting) to steer you to the narrow agent, and hide agents known to fail in vivo.Call the micro lab if you genuinely need the hidden result — don't assume the drug wasn't tested.
Oxacillin R on a staph panelThis is the MRSA readout — mecA/PBP2a. Oxacillin is the surrogate tested for all β-lactams.Every β-lactam fails except ceftaroline, irrespective of what other β-lactam MICs appear.
Erythromycin R, clindamycin SPossible inducible erm-mediated resistance.Ask for the D-test. If positive, clindamycin will fail on therapy — pick something else.
Get the cultures before the first dose — but never delay antibiotics in septic shock to get them. Two sets of blood cultures from two separate sites before antibiotics roughly doubles the yield and is what lets you de-escalate on day 3. A single positive coagulase-negative staph bottle out of four is contamination; the same organism in both sets, or in a patient with prosthetic material, is not.
Shared

Penicillin allergy

⚠️

The most consequential wrong label in medicine

About 10% of the population carries a penicillin-allergy label, and more than 90–95% of them are not allergic. Some never were — the "rash" was the viral exanthem that brought them to the doctor in the first place, or an ampicillin rash during EBV infection. Others were, but IgE wanes: roughly half of genuinely IgE-sensitised patients lose reactivity by 5 years and about 80% by 10 years.

That label is not harmless. Patients labelled penicillin-allergic receive more vancomycin, fluoroquinolones and clindamycin; they have measurably more C. difficile, more MRSA and VRE, longer stays, and worse surgical-site infection rates. Delabelling is an intervention, not a formality.

What the patient describesWhat it probably isWhat you can safely do
"Rash as a child, no details, decades ago"Usually a viral exanthem or a benign delayed maculopapular eruption — not IgE-mediated.Direct oral challenge (an observed amoxicillin dose) is now the recommended pathway for low-risk histories; skin testing first is not required. Cephalosporins can be given without hesitation.
Isolated GI upset, nausea, diarrhoea, headache, yeast infectionAn intolerance, not an allergy.Not an allergy at all — remove the label and prescribe penicillins freely.
Delayed benign maculopapular rash days into a course, no mucosal involvementA T-cell-mediated delayed reaction. Low risk of anaphylaxis.Cephalosporins and carbapenems are safe. Penicillin can often be re-challenged with allergy input.
Hives, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension, throat tightness within 1 hourGenuine IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity.Avoid penicillins. Use a cephalosporin with a dissimilar R1 side chain (cefazolin, ceftriaxone, cefepime — all safe), a carbapenem (<1% cross-reactivity), or aztreonam. Refer to allergy for testing.
Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, AGEP, serum sickness, interstitial nephritis, haemolytic anaemiaA severe non-IgE reaction.Absolute contraindication to the whole β-lactam class — never test, never challenge, never desensitise. Use a structurally unrelated class entirely.
Cross-reactivity is about the side chain, not the ring. The old "10% cross-reactivity with cephalosporins" figure came from 1960s–70s studies using cephalosporins contaminated with penicillin during manufacture. Modern data put it at roughly 1–2% or less, and the risk tracks R1 side-chain similarity. Amoxicillin shares an R1 side chain with cefadroxil, cefprozil and cefatrizine; ampicillin shares one with cephalexin, cefaclor and cephradine. Those are the cephalosporins to avoid. Cefazolin has a unique side chain shared with no penicillin and no other cephalosporin — it is the safest cephalosporin in penicillin allergy and can be given even to many patients with documented penicillin anaphylaxis.
If the patient truly cannot have a penicillin, use…Instead of…Note
Cefazolin 2 g IV q8h · ceftriaxone 1–2 g q24h · cefepime 2 g q8hNafcillin, ampicillin, pip-tazoUnique or dissimilar R1 side chains — safe in nearly all penicillin-allergic patients including many with anaphylaxis histories.
Aztreonam 2 g IV q8hAny gram-negative β-lactamMonocyclic — essentially no penicillin cross-reactivity. Except: avoid if the reaction was to ceftazidime (identical R1 side chain). No gram-positive or anaerobic coverage — always needs a partner.
Meropenem 1 g IV q8hPip-tazoThe 2022 drug-allergy practice parameter states a carbapenem may be given to a penicillin- or cephalosporin-allergic patient without testing or additional precautions. Cross-reactivity is negligible.
Vancomycin, linezolid, daptomycin, clindamycinCefazolin/nafcillin for gram-positive coverThe non-β-lactam gram-positive options for severe allergy.
Levofloxacin, aztreonam, aminoglycoside, TMP-SMXCeftriaxone for gram-negative coverChoose by site and susceptibility. Add metronidazole if anaerobes matter.
Desensitisation (in an ICU with an allergist)—Reserve for when the β-lactam is truly irreplaceable: syphilis in pregnancy, MSSA or enterococcal endocarditis, neurosyphilis. Induces temporary tolerance only — it is lost within about 48 h of stopping. Never attempt after SJS/TEN/DRESS.
🧮

PEN-FAST — is this penicillin allergy label safe to challenge?

A validated bedside rule for non-allergists. Entry criterion: the patient reports a penicillin allergy.

Five years or less since the reaction +2
Anaphylaxis or angioedema, or Severe cutaneous adverse reaction +2
Treatment was required for the reaction +1
Bands
0 — very low risk (~<1% positive)
1–2 — low risk (~5%)
3 — moderate risk (~20%)
4–5 — high risk (~50%)
A score <3 carries a negative predictive value of roughly 96% for a genuinely positive penicillin allergy test.
0
PEN-FAST identifies who can go straight to a direct oral amoxicillin challenge without skin testing. It does not replace allergy referral for high scores, and it does not apply to severe cutaneous adverse reactions, which are an absolute contraindication regardless of score.

Comorbidities, organ dysfunction & interactions

🔗

How comorbidity changes both the bug and the drug

ComorbidityHow it changes the infectionHow it changes the antibiotic
Diabetes mellitusImpaired neutrophil function and microvascular disease → more severe and more polymicrobial infection. Diabetic foot infection is classically mixed aerobic gram-positive + gram-negative + anaerobe. Higher MRSA carriage. Higher risk of emphysematous pyelonephritis/cholecystitis, malignant otitis externa (Pseudomonas), and mucormycosis in DKA. Neuropathy masks pain, so infections present late and deep.Broaden for chronic, previously treated, or severe foot infection: add anaerobic coverage for ischaemic/necrotic/malodorous wounds, MRSA coverage for prior MRSA or severe disease, and Pseudomonas coverage for macerated/water-exposed wounds, warm climates, or prior Pseudomonas. Avoid fluoroquinolones where possible (dysglycaemia — both hypo- and hyperglycaemia). Always probe to bone and image before assuming soft tissue only.
CKD / AKIUraemia impairs immunity; dialysis catheters are a major S. aureus bacteraemia source.Dose-adjust nearly everything (see the table below). Cefepime neurotoxicity and carbapenem seizures are almost always the consequence of an unadjusted dose. Avoid nitrofurantoin below CrCl 30. Watch TMP-SMX hyperkalaemia. Vancomycin + pip-tazo and aminoglycosides compound nephrotoxicity — use AUC-guided vancomycin dosing and stop aminoglycosides early.
CirrhosisImpaired reticuloendothelial clearance, gut translocation, and hypocomplementaemic ascites → spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and infection is a leading trigger of acute-on-chronic liver failure. Threshold for infection is far lower.Ceftriaxone is the SBP workhorse (2 g IV q24h ×5 d) with albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1 and 1 g/kg day 3. Avoid aminoglycosides entirely (very high hepatorenal syndrome risk). Watch amox-clav and TMP-SMX hepatotoxicity; monitor for prolonged QT with macrolides in advanced disease.
Heart failure / structural heart diseaseHigher endocarditis risk with prosthetic valves and devices; congestion complicates volume management during sepsis resuscitation.Watch the sodium load of high-dose IV β-lactams and the volume of large-volume infusions. Macrolides and fluoroquinolones prolong the QT in a population already on amiodarone/sotalol — check a baseline ECG.
Advanced age (>65)Blunted fever and leukocytosis; delirium may be the only presenting sign; higher rates of resistant organisms from healthcare exposure.Creatinine overestimates GFR when muscle mass is low — calculate CrCl, don't eyeball the creatinine. Highest C. difficile risk. Avoid fluoroquinolones (delirium, tendon rupture, aortic events) where an alternative exists. Watch cefepime neurotoxicity.
Neutropenia / immunosuppressionFever may be the only sign; classic findings (infiltrate, pus, meningismus) may be absent because there are no neutrophils to make them. Viridans strep, Pseudomonas and fungi become real threats.Bactericidal, antipseudomonal, and immediate — antibiotics within an hour of the first fever. Do not wait for a source. Add antifungal coverage for persistent fever at 4–7 days.
Seizure disorder—Meropenem drops valproate levels by 60–100% and has caused breakthrough status epilepticus — avoid the combination. Imipenem has the highest intrinsic seizure risk; cefepime and fluoroquinolones lower the seizure threshold.
Myasthenia gravis—Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and telithromycin — all can precipitate a myasthenic crisis by impairing neuromuscular transmission. β-lactams are safe.
On warfarin—TMP-SMX (CYP2C9 inhibition + protein displacement) and metronidazole are the most dangerous; fluoroquinolones, macrolides and azoles also raise the INR. Any antibiotic that wipes gut flora reduces vitamin K₂. Check the INR within 3–5 days of starting and consider a pre-emptive dose reduction. Conversely, rifampin and nafcillin induce metabolism and cause loss of anticoagulation.
Transplant / calcineurin inhibitorsAtypical and opportunistic pathogens; blunted inflammatory response.Rifampin destroys tacrolimus/cyclosporine levels and can precipitate rejection. Clarithromycin and azoles do the opposite — they raise levels toward toxicity. Coordinate with transplant pharmacy before any of these.
G6PD deficiency—Avoid TMP-SMX, nitrofurantoin, dapsone and primaquine — oxidative haemolysis.
Prosthetic joint / device / hardwareBiofilm makes organisms phenotypically tolerant to almost every antibiotic; cure often requires hardware removal.Add rifampin 300–450 mg PO BID for staphylococcal infection with retained hardware (biofilm penetration) — always with a companion drug, never alone. Prolonged therapy and surgical planning are the rule.
ObesityHigher SSTI and surgical-site infection rates.Under-dosing is the commonest error: cefazolin 2–3 g (not 1 g), vancomycin loading on actual body weight, aminoglycosides on adjusted body weight. Fixed-dose agents (ertapenem, ceftriaxone) may under-perform at extremes of weight.
PregnancyAsymptomatic bacteriuria must be treated (unlike in non-pregnant adults) — untreated it progresses to pyelonephritis and preterm labour.Safe: penicillins, cephalosporins, azithromycin, clindamycin, metronidazole (after the first trimester by convention). Avoid: fluoroquinolones (cartilage), tetracyclines (teeth/bone, maternal hepatotoxicity), TMP-SMX (neural-tube defects in the first trimester; kernicterus near term), aminoglycosides (fetal ototoxicity). Nitrofurantoin is acceptable in the second trimester but avoided at term and in the first trimester where alternatives exist.
Drugs to avoid — the list worth committing to memory.
  • Daptomycin for pneumonia — inactivated by surfactant. It will fail.
  • Vancomycin for MSSA — inferior to cefazolin/nafcillin; de-escalate the moment you know.
  • Ceftriaxone for Enterobacter/Serratia/Citrobacter — AmpC de-repression and mid-course relapse.
  • Nitrofurantoin for pyelonephritis or bacteraemia — no tissue or serum levels.
  • Moxifloxacin for UTI — does not reach therapeutic urinary concentrations.
  • Ciprofloxacin for cellulitis or pneumonia — no meaningful streptococcal or pneumococcal activity.
  • Tigecycline for bacteraemia, pneumonia or UTI — boxed mortality warning and inadequate serum/urine levels.
  • Cephalexin or clindamycin alone for an animal bite — both miss Pasteurella.
  • Any cephalosporin for Enterococcus or Listeria — intrinsic resistance.
  • Meropenem with valproate — breakthrough seizures.
  • Rifampin as monotherapy — resistance emerges within days.
  • Metronidazole added to pip-tazo, a carbapenem, or cefoxitin — redundant anaerobic coverage with pure added toxicity.

🧮

Creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault) — the number antibiotic dosing actually uses

Nearly every antibiotic renal-dosing table is built on Cockcroft-Gault CrCl in mL/min, not on the eGFR your lab reports. They are not interchangeable — eGFR is normalised to 1.73 m² body surface area, which systematically misestimates dosing requirements at the extremes of body size.

—
CrCl = [(140 − age) × weight] ÷ (72 × Cr) × 0.85 if female. Use actual body weight in normal-weight patients; many pharmacies use adjusted body weight if >30% over ideal.

C. difficile risk by agent

Every antibiotic can cause C. difficile, but the risk is far from uniform. The pattern tracks how thoroughly the drug wipes out protective anaerobic colonic flora.

Risk tierAgentsWhy
HighestClindamycin; fluoroquinolones; 3rd- and 4th-generation cephalosporins; carbapenemsProfound and prolonged disruption of colonic anaerobes with no activity against C. difficile itself. Fluoroquinolone use drove the epidemic NAP1/BI/027 strain.
IntermediateBroad-spectrum penicillins (amox-clav, pip-tazo); 1st- and 2nd-generation cephalosporins; macrolidesMeaningful flora disruption but less complete.
LowestDoxycycline/tetracyclines; TMP-SMX; aminoglycosides; nitrofurantoin; IV vancomycin; metronidazole; daptomycin; linezolidLittle colonic anaerobic disruption; some (doxycycline, metronidazole) have direct anti-clostridial activity.
Risk is driven more by days of therapy and by number of agents than by any single drug choice, and remains elevated for around three months after the course ends. The most effective C. difficile prevention available to you is stopping antibiotics on time.

Major drug interactions

CombinationWhat happensWhat to do
TMP-SMX + warfarinMarked INR rise and bleeding.Check INR in 3–5 days; many clinicians pre-emptively reduce the warfarin dose by 25–50% or choose another antibiotic.
TMP-SMX + ACEi/ARB/spironolactoneLife-threatening hyperkalaemia — trimethoprim blocks the distal ENaC channel.Check K⁺ within 3–7 days; avoid in advanced CKD.
TMP-SMX + methotrexateAdditive antifolate effect → pancytopenia.Avoid the combination.
Linezolid + SSRI/SNRI/MAOI/triptansSerotonin syndrome (linezolid is a weak reversible MAO inhibitor).Ideally hold the serotonergic agent; if not possible, monitor closely for clonus, hyperthermia and agitation.
Rifampin + almost anythingPotent CYP3A4/2C9 and P-glycoprotein induction — loss of efficacy of warfarin, DOACs, oral contraceptives, tacrolimus, azoles, protease inhibitors, methadone.Review the entire med list before the first dose; arrange alternative contraception.
Clarithromycin/erythromycin + statins, colchicine, calcineurin inhibitorsCYP3A4 inhibition → rhabdomyolysis, colchicine toxicity, transplant drug toxicity.Use azithromycin instead (minimal CYP effect), or hold the statin.
Fluoroquinolones/macrolides + amiodarone, sotalol, antipsychotics, ondansetronAdditive QT prolongation → torsades.Baseline ECG, correct K⁺ and Mg²⁺, avoid stacking.
Meropenem + valproateValproate levels fall 60–100% within 24–48 h → breakthrough seizures.Avoid; if unavoidable, use an alternative anticonvulsant and monitor levels.
Fluoroquinolones/tetracyclines + calcium, magnesium, iron, zinc, sucralfate, antacids, tube feedsChelation blocks absorption and causes silent treatment failure.Give 2 h before or 6 h after; hold tube feeds around the dose.
Metronidazole + alcoholDisulfiram-like reaction (flushing, vomiting, tachycardia).Counsel to avoid alcohol during and for 3 days after.
Nafcillin + warfarin/tacrolimusCYP induction → subtherapeutic levels (the mirror image of the usual antibiotic–warfarin problem).Monitor INR/levels closely and expect to increase doses.
🩺 Clinic — outpatient infections, oral regimens & when it is safe to stay home
Assess

Does this patient need an antibiotic at all?

🔍

The first and most important question in ambulatory infectious disease

Roughly a third of outpatient antibiotic prescriptions in the US are unnecessary, and most of that is respiratory. Before you write anything, decide whether this is bacterial, whether it will resolve without treatment, and whether the harm of treating exceeds the benefit.

PresentationAntibiotic?Reasoning
Acute bronchitis / cough <3 weeks, no COPDNo>90% viral. Purulent sputum reflects sloughed inflammatory cells, not bacterial infection. Antibiotics shorten cough by less than a day and cause harm in roughly 1 in 5.
Upper respiratory infection / "sinus pressure" <10 daysNoViral rhinosinusitis peaks at 3–6 days and resolves. Treat only with ≥10 days without improvement, severe symptoms (fever ≥39 °C + purulent discharge) for ≥3–4 days, or "double worsening" — improvement then deterioration.
Sore throat, Centor/McIsaac 0–1NoTest only if 2–3 points; treat only if the rapid antigen test or culture is positive. Antibiotics for strep pharyngitis exist chiefly to prevent acute rheumatic fever, not to shorten symptoms.
Asymptomatic bacteriuriaNoTreating it does not prevent symptomatic UTI and does cause resistance and C. difficile. Exceptions: pregnancy and before an invasive urologic procedure with expected mucosal bleeding. Do not send a urine culture in a patient with no urinary symptoms.
Chronic leg swelling, bilateral, no feverUsually noBilateral "cellulitis" is almost always stasis dermatitis or lipodermatosclerosis. True cellulitis is nearly always unilateral. Around a third of admitted "cellulitis" is a mimic.
Simple cutaneous abscess, drainedOften yes nowIncision and drainage is the treatment; two randomised trials (Talan 2016 and Daum 2017) showed adding TMP-SMX or clindamycin improves cure by roughly 7–10 percentage points, so most patients should get an oral agent.
Uncomplicated diverticulitis, immunocompetent, wellOften noThe AVOD and DIABOLO randomised trials found no benefit of antibiotics; guidelines now support selective, not routine, use in mild disease with reliable follow-up.
Fever + focal findings + systemic illnessYesCulture first where feasible, then treat with the narrowest agent that covers the likely pathogens for that site.
CulturesWound culture after I&D if purulent, severe, recurrent, or in an immunocompromised patient. Urine culture for pyelonephritis, complicated UTI, recurrent cystitis, pregnancy, or treatment failure — not for uncomplicated first-episode cystitis in a healthy woman.Before abx
Rapid strep / throat cultureCentor/McIsaac ≥2. Treat only if positive. Back-up culture in children and adolescents if the rapid test is negative.If indicated
CBC, BMPIf systemically unwell, at extremes of age, or before starting an agent needing renal dosing. Establishes a baseline creatinine and potassium before TMP-SMX.Selective
Chest radiographRequired to diagnose pneumonia — a clinical diagnosis alone over-treats. Order for cough with fever, tachypnoea, hypoxia, or focal exam findings.If CAP suspected
ProcalcitoninReasonable in ambiguous lower respiratory tract infection to support withholding antibiotics — but only alongside clinical judgement, never instead of it.Optional
HIV, glucose/HbA1cRecurrent or unusually severe skin, respiratory or oral infection warrants screening for an undiagnosed immunocompromising condition.Recurrent infection
Delayed or "safety-net" prescribing — giving the patient a prescription with instructions to fill it only if they are not better in 2–3 days — reduces antibiotic use substantially without increasing complications in sinusitis, otitis and bronchitis. It is often the right compromise when a patient expects a prescription and the clinical picture does not justify one.
Treat

Oral regimens by syndrome

💊

Preferred · alternative · penicillin-allergic — with dose, frequency and duration

Non-purulent cellulitis. Unilateral, spreading, warm erythema with indistinct borders. No fluctuance, no drainage — this is a streptococcal disease, and empiric MRSA coverage is not indicated.
Image: Left cellulitis of leg.jpg — Stephen Ewen, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

Non-purulent cellulitis / erysipelas — target: β-haemolytic streptococci

Non-purulent cellulitis is overwhelmingly streptococcal, not staphylococcal. Adding MRSA coverage to a simple cellulitis does not improve cure rates and adds toxicity — a randomised trial of cephalexin versus cephalexin + TMP-SMX showed no difference. Cover strep, and cover staph only if there is pus.
TierRegimenDurationWhyIf penicillin-allergic
PreferredCephalexin 500 mg PO QID (or 1 g PO TID)5 days, extended only if not improvingCovers strep and MSSA; the 5-day course was shown non-inferior to 10 days in a randomised trial.Clindamycin 300–450 mg PO QID, or doxycycline 100 mg PO BID (adds MRSA), or linezolid 600 mg PO BID.
AlternativesDicloxacillin 500 mg PO QID · penicillin VK 500 mg PO QID (for classic erysipelas) · amoxicillin 500 mg PO TID5–7 daysPenicillin VK is the narrowest option when the picture is unmistakably erysipelas (sharply demarcated, raised, fiery-red).As above.
Add MRSA coverage if…Add TMP-SMX 1–2 DS PO BID or doxycycline 100 mg BID to the cephalexin5–7 daysPenetrating trauma, injection drug use, known MRSA colonisation, purulent drainage, SIRS, or failure of β-lactam monotherapy.Clindamycin or linezolid monotherapy covers both.
AdjunctsElevate the limb (as effective as any drug), mark the border with a pen and date it, treat tinea pedis and venous stasis (the usual portal of entry), and control oedema — this is how you prevent recurrence.

Purulent SSTI / cutaneous abscess — target: S. aureus including MRSA

TierRegimenDurationWhyNotes
The treatmentIncision and drainage—Drainage is the therapy; antibiotics are the adjunct. No antibiotic cures an undrained abscess.Send a wound culture — this is how your region's MRSA rate gets known.
Preferred adjunctTMP-SMX 1–2 DS tabs PO BID5–7 days (10 days in the trials)Talan (NEJM 2016) showed cure 80.5% with TMP-SMX vs 73.6% with placebo after I&D; Daum (NEJM 2017) showed clindamycin and TMP-SMX both beat placebo for small abscesses.Check K⁺/creatinine in the elderly or on ACEi/ARB.
AlternativesDoxycycline 100 mg PO BID · clindamycin 300–450 mg PO QID · linezolid 600 mg PO BID5–10 daysDoxycycline is well tolerated and cheap. Clindamycin adds strep coverage but carries the highest C. difficile risk.Doxycycline: avoid in pregnancy and children <8. Clindamycin: check the D-test.

Animal and human bites — target: Pasteurella, Eikenella, staph, strep, oral anaerobes

ScenarioRegimenDurationNotes
Prophylaxis (fresh bite, high-risk)Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID3–5 daysHigh-risk = cat bites (deep punctures), hand/face/genital bites, crush injuries, immunocompromise, asplenia, cirrhosis, prosthetic joints.
Established infectionAmox-clav 875 mg PO BID; IV ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g q6h if severe5–14 daysGet imaging for retained tooth/foreign body; involve hand surgery for any closed-fist "fight bite" over the MCP joints.
Penicillin-allergicDoxycycline 100 mg PO BID or a fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX, plus metronidazole 500 mg PO TID or clindamycin for anaerobesSameCephalexin, dicloxacillin and clindamycin alone all miss Pasteurella — the single most common bite-wound prescribing error.
Always alsoTetanus status, rabies risk assessment for wild/unvaccinated animals, copious irrigation, and consider leaving the wound open rather than primary closure (except on the face).
Pain out of proportion to the exam, rapid progression over hours, bullae, skin anaesthesia, crepitus, a dusky or violaceous hue, or systemic toxicity means necrotising soft-tissue infection. This is a surgical emergency — do not manage it in clinic, do not wait for imaging, and send the patient to the ED for immediate surgical consultation.

Community-acquired pneumonia — outpatient (ATS/IDSA 2019)

PatientPreferredAlternativesDurationWhy
No comorbidities, no recent antibioticsAmoxicillin 1 g PO TID or doxycycline 100 mg PO BIDA macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg day 1 then 250 mg daily ×4 d) only where local pneumococcal macrolide resistance is below 25%Minimum 5 days, and until afebrile 48 h with ≤1 abnormal clinical-stability criterionHigh-dose amoxicillin covers pneumococcus including intermediate-penicillin-resistance (a PBP-affinity problem that more drug overcomes). Doxycycline additionally covers atypicals.
With comorbidities — chronic heart, lung, liver or renal disease; diabetes; alcohol use disorder; malignancy; asplenia; or antibiotics in the last 90 daysAmox-clav 875/125 mg PO BID (or 2000/125 mg BID) or a cephalosporin (cefpodoxime 200 mg BID / cefuroxime 500 mg BID) PLUS a macrolide or doxycycline 100 mg BIDRespiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy: levofloxacin 750 mg PO daily or moxifloxacin 400 mg PO dailyMinimum 5 daysThe β-lactam covers pneumococcus, H. influenzae and MSSA; the macrolide/doxycycline covers Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydia. A respiratory quinolone covers both in one drug — reserve it, because of the boxed warnings and C. difficile risk.
The 2019 ATS/IDSA guideline abandoned the term "healthcare-associated pneumonia" (HCAP) — it over-predicted resistant organisms and drove enormous unnecessary vancomycin and pip-tazo use. Cover MRSA or Pseudomonas only for prior isolation of that organism, or hospitalisation with parenteral antibiotics within 90 days plus locally validated risk factors.

Outpatient pyelonephritis is safe when the patient is haemodynamically stable, can keep down oral fluids and medication, is not pregnant, has no obstruction (no stone, no hydronephrosis, no indwelling hardware), is not severely immunocompromised, and has follow-up within 48–72 hours. Anything else — vomiting, hypotension, obstruction, sepsis, pregnancy, or male sex with suspected prostatitis needing prolonged therapy — goes inpatient.
Men, catheters and recurrence. UTI in a man is by definition complicated; consider prostatitis and use an agent that penetrates prostate (fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX) for 10–14 days (up to 6 weeks in chronic bacterial prostatitis). For catheter-associated UTI, exchange or remove the catheter before or at the start of therapy — otherwise you are treating a biofilm you cannot reach.

Decide

When outpatient management is safe

🏡

The clinical case for staying home — and the biomarker case

Two independent questions decide disposition, and you must answer both. Clinically: can this patient's physiology tolerate the infection, can they take and absorb an oral drug, and is the source controlled? Biochemically: does the trajectory support de-escalation or stopping? A reassuring biomarker never overrides an unwell patient, and a normal-looking patient with an undrained abscess is not safe at home no matter what the labs say.

The clinical checklist — every box must be ticked

DomainThreshold to be safe at homeWhy it matters
HaemodynamicsSBP ≥90 mmHg without fluids or pressors; HR ≤100Hypotension is the single strongest predictor of deterioration and mandates admission regardless of how well the patient looks.
Oxygenation & respirationSpO₂ ≥90% on room air (or at the patient's known baseline); RR ≤24Tachypnoea is the earliest and most sensitive vital-sign abnormality in sepsis, and is routinely under-recorded.
Temperature≤37.8 °C, or clearly trending down over 24 hSustained fever after 48–72 h of appropriate therapy means an undrained source, a resistant organism, a wrong diagnosis, or drug fever.
MentationAt the patient's baselineNew confusion, particularly in the elderly, may be the only manifestation of sepsis.
Oral intakeTolerating oral fluids and medication; no vomiting; functioning gutAn excellent oral regimen the patient vomits is no regimen at all.
Source controlAbscess drained, catheter removed or exchanged, obstruction relieved, necrotic tissue debridedThe most common reason "the antibiotics aren't working" is that the source was never controlled. No antibiotic sterilises an undrained collection.
The drug itselfAn oral agent exists that covers the organism, the patient can afford it and obtain it, and interactions have been checkedCost and pharmacy access are clinical variables — an unfilled prescription is a treatment failure.
Follow-upReassessment within 48–72 h arranged, with explicit return precautionsOutpatient management is a plan, not a discharge. The patient must know exactly what would make them come back.
HostNot neutropenic, not pregnant with pyelonephritis, no unstable comorbidity, no prosthetic material at the infected siteThese hosts fail quietly and fast.
🧮

CURB-65 — pneumonia severity and site of care

One point for each criterion present. Use it to support a decision to treat at home, never to override a clinical impression that the patient is unwell.

Confusion (new disorientation) +1
Urea >7 mmol/L (BUN >19 mg/dL) +1
Respiratory rate ≥30/min +1
Blood pressure: SBP <90 or DBP ≤60 +1
Age ≥65 years +1
0
CURB-65 is weighted heavily toward age and will under-call severity in a young patient with a high oxygen requirement. The ATS/IDSA guideline prefers the PSI/PORT score for the outpatient-versus-inpatient decision because it is better validated for identifying low-risk patients — it is a 20-variable weighted model, so use a calculator rather than estimating it: PSI/PORT on MDCalc. Neither score assesses hypoxia adequately, and neither accounts for social factors: an unhoused patient, someone unable to obtain the medication, or someone with no one to check on them may need admission with a CURB-65 of 0.

Procalcitonin — using it honestly

Procalcitonin is a precursor of calcitonin released by parenchymal tissues throughout the body in response to bacterial endotoxin and the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, TNF-α and IL-6. Interferon-γ, released in viral infection, actively suppresses it — which is the mechanism behind its bacterial-versus-viral discrimination. It begins rising at 3–4 hours, peaks at 6–24 hours, and falls with a half-life of roughly 24 hours, making it useful for tracking a trajectory.

PCT (ng/mL)Interpretation in lower respiratory tract infectionAction
<0.10Bacterial infection very unlikelyStrongly discourage antibiotics
0.10–0.25Bacterial infection unlikelyDiscourage antibiotics
0.25–0.50Bacterial infection possibleEncourage antibiotics
>0.50Bacterial infection likelyStrongly encourage antibiotics
The stopping rule. Therapy is discontinued when procalcitonin falls below 0.25 ng/mL (the respiratory-infection algorithms) or below 0.5 ng/mL (the ICU algorithms), or drops by at least 80% from its peak. Applied inside a protocol this works: ProHOSP cut mean antibiotic exposure from 8.7 to 5.7 days with fewer antibiotic adverse effects (19.8% vs 28.1%) and no excess mortality; PRORATA gained 2.7 antibiotic-free days in the ICU; SAPS shortened therapy from 7 to 5 days. But ProACT — 1,656 patients across 14 US hospitals — found no difference at all (4.2 versus 4.3 antibiotic-days), because US baseline durations were already short and clinicians simply overrode the result. Procalcitonin removes excess duration; where duration is already appropriate it adds nothing, and it only ever helps if you act on it.
Where procalcitonin lies to you.
  • Falsely HIGH without bacterial infection: renal failure and dialysis (reduced clearance), major surgery, trauma, burns, cardiac arrest and post-resuscitation, cardiogenic shock, pancreatitis, medullary thyroid carcinoma and small-cell lung cancer, the first 48 h of life, anti-thymocyte globulin and IL-2 therapy, severe malaria, heat stroke.
  • Falsely LOW despite real bacterial infection: localised, walled-off infection — abscess, empyema, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, mediastinitis; early infection before the 3–4 hour rise; and infection in a profoundly immunosuppressed host.
  • Never useful for: deciding whether an abscess needs drainage, diagnosing C. difficile, or distinguishing colonisation from infection.
A normal procalcitonin in a patient with a drainable collection is a trap. PCT supports a decision; it never makes one.

CRP and ESR are far less specific — CRP rises in any inflammatory state, peaks at 36–50 hours, and has a half-life of ~19 hours; ESR changes over days to weeks and is more useful for following osteomyelitis or endocarditis than for acute decisions. Neither distinguishes bacterial from non-bacterial inflammation reliably enough to start or stop antibiotics on its own.

Monitor

Follow-up, duration & failure

📈

What to recheck and when

WhenWhat to reassessWhat a bad answer means
48–72 hoursFever curve, pain, erythema border (marked and dated), oral tolerance, culture results now back.No improvement by 72 h = wrong bug, wrong drug, undrained source, wrong diagnosis (DVT, gout, stasis dermatitis, drug reaction), or an adherence/absorption problem. Re-examine before you broaden.
3–7 days (on TMP-SMX, ACEi/ARB, CKD, elderly)Potassium and creatinine.Hyperkalaemia from trimethoprim's ENaC blockade; a creatinine rise that may be a benign secretion artefact rather than true AKI.
3–5 days (on warfarin)INR.TMP-SMX, metronidazole, fluoroquinolones and macrolides all raise it; nafcillin and rifampin lower it.
End of courseSymptom resolution. Repeat cultures only where they change management.Do not obtain a test-of-cure urine culture in an asymptomatic patient after cystitis — it drives treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria.
Weekly (linezolid >2 weeks)CBC; ask about vision and paraesthesias.Thrombocytopenia, anaemia, optic and peripheral neuropathy.
Weekly (daptomycin)CPK.Myopathy — hold statins during therapy.
Any timeNew diarrhoea.Consider C. difficile — but only test if ≥3 unformed stools in 24 h and no laxatives.

Evidence-based durations — shorter is almost always right

The single biggest change in antibiotic practice over the last two decades is that nearly every course we were taught is longer than it needs to be. Longer courses do not prevent relapse; they select resistance and cause harm.

InfectionDurationNote
Community-acquired pneumonia5 days minimum, stop once clinically stable and afebrile 48 hA randomised trial of 3 days of β-lactam after early improvement found non-inferiority — the direction of travel is shorter still.
Hospital-acquired / ventilator-associated pneumonia7 daysEquivalent to 15 days with less resistance emergence; applies even to non-fermenting gram-negatives per the 2016 IDSA/ATS guideline.
Uncomplicated cystitis3 days TMP-SMX · 5 days nitrofurantoin · 1 dose fosfomycin—
Pyelonephritis5 days levofloxacin 750 · 7 days ciprofloxacin · 10–14 days β-lactam or TMP-SMX—
Cellulitis5–6 days if improvingExtend only for slow response; the randomised comparison of 5 vs 10 days found no difference.
Intra-abdominal infection after source control4 daysThe STOP-IT trial: a fixed 4-day course after adequate source control matched treating until 2 days after physiologic normalisation.
Uncomplicated gram-negative bacteraemia7 daysNon-inferior to 14 days in randomised trials, provided the source is controlled and the patient has responded.
COPD exacerbation5 days—
Acute bacterial sinusitis5–7 days in adults—
Strep pharyngitis10 daysOne of the few genuinely long courses — the duration is set by rheumatic-fever prevention, not symptom relief.
C. difficile10 days—
S. aureus bacteraemia≥14 days uncomplicated · 4–6 weeks complicatedNever short-course. Always get ID involved, repeat blood cultures to document clearance, and echocardiography.
"Finish the whole course" is outdated advice for most infections. The idea that stopping early breeds resistance was never supported by evidence; the opposite is true — every extra day of exposure selects resistant organisms in the patient's own flora. The modern instruction is: take it exactly as prescribed for the duration prescribed, and the duration prescribed should be the shortest one the evidence supports.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B, vaccines & ambulatory stewardship

🛡️

Grade A & B recommendations relevant to infection

GradeRecommendationPopulation
AScreen for HIVAdolescents and adults aged 15–65; younger and older at increased risk; all pregnant persons.

AScreen for syphilisPersons at increased risk; all pregnant persons (early in pregnancy).

BScreen for hepatitis BAdolescents and adults at increased risk.
BScreen for chlamydia and gonorrhoeaSexually active women 24 and younger, and older women at increased risk.

BScreen for asymptomatic bacteriuria with urine culturePregnant persons — the one population where treating asymptomatic bacteriuria is clearly beneficial. USPSTF recommends against screening non-pregnant adults (Grade D).

Vaccines that prevent the infections in this guide

VaccineWhoWhy it belongs in an antibiotic guide
Pneumococcal (PCV20, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23)All adults ≥50, and adults 19–49 with chronic heart/lung/liver/kidney disease, diabetes, smoking, alcohol use disorder, cochlear implant, CSF leak, asplenia or immunocompromise.Directly reduces the pneumococcal pneumonia and bacteraemia that drive most CAP antibiotic use.
Influenza (annual)Everyone ≥6 months.Influenza is the setup for post-influenza bacterial pneumonia — classically S. aureus, pneumococcus and Group A strep. Preventing flu prevents the superinfection.
COVID-19Per current CDC schedule.Reduces hospitalisation, and therefore healthcare exposure and MDRO acquisition.
RSVAdults ≥75, and 50–74 at increased risk.Prevents a viral LRTI that is routinely and unnecessarily treated with antibiotics.
Tdap / TdTdap once, then Td or Tdap every 10 years; Tdap in every pregnancy.Tetanus prophylaxis is part of every bite and wound encounter.
Recombinant zosterAdults ≥50, and immunocompromised adults ≥19.Prevents zoster and its secondary bacterial skin infection.
Meningococcal + HibAsplenia (including sickle cell), complement deficiency, and anyone on eculizumab/ravulizumab.These patients are at extreme risk of fulminant encapsulated-organism sepsis and need standing antibiotic action plans as well as vaccines.
Ambulatory stewardship is mostly a communication skill. The interventions with the best evidence are not clinical: naming a specific diagnosis ("this is a viral bronchitis"), giving a symptom timeline so the patient knows what normal recovery looks like, offering a delayed prescription, providing a written care plan, and — for clinicians — public commitment posters and peer-comparison feedback on prescribing rates. Antibiotic expectations are far more often assumed by the clinician than actually held by the patient.
Escalate

Red flags — send to the ED

🚑

Do not manage these in clinic

Physiology: SBP <90 or a drop >40 from baseline · HR >120 · RR ≥22 with any confusion (qSOFA ≥2) · SpO₂ <90% on room air · new confusion or reduced consciousness · temperature <36 °C (hypothermia is more ominous than fever) · lactate ≥2 mmol/L if available · mottling or prolonged capillary refill.
Syndromes that need the ED now, not an oral prescription:
  • Necrotising soft-tissue infection — pain out of proportion, rapid progression, bullae, crepitus, skin anaesthesia, dusky skin, systemic toxicity. Surgical emergency.
  • Meningitis — fever with headache, neck stiffness, photophobia or altered mentation. Antibiotics and dexamethasone must not wait for the LP or CT.
  • Febrile neutropenia — any fever in a patient on chemotherapy within the last 6 weeks. Antibiotics within 1 hour.
  • Obstructed infected urinary tract — pyelonephritis with a known stone, hydronephrosis, or anuria. Needs decompression, not just antibiotics.
  • Ascending cholangitis — fever, jaundice and RUQ pain (Charcot's triad), with hypotension and confusion (Reynolds' pentad) marking severe disease. Needs urgent biliary drainage.
  • Septic arthritis — an acutely hot, swollen, exquisitely painful joint. Needs aspiration before antibiotics and often washout.
  • Endocarditis — persistent fever with a new murmur, embolic phenomena, injection drug use, or prosthetic valve/device.
  • Orbital or periorbital cellulitis with proptosis, pain on eye movement, or vision change; Ludwig's angina or any deep neck-space infection with trismus, drooling or voice change — both are airway emergencies.
  • Fournier's gangrene — perineal pain, swelling or crepitus, particularly in a diabetic patient.
Failure of outpatient therapy — no improvement or worsening after 48–72 h of appropriate oral antibiotics — warrants re-evaluation in person, not a phoned-in broader prescription. Before you escalate the drug, escalate the thinking: is there an undrained collection, a resistant organism, a non-infectious mimic, an absorption failure, or an adherence problem?
🛏️ Wards — empiric IV therapy by organ system, IV→PO switch & de-escalation
Admit

Who needs IV antibiotics

📋

The route decision is separate from the admission decision

Residents routinely conflate two different questions. "Does this patient need to be in hospital?" is about physiology, monitoring, and social support. "Does this patient need intravenous antibiotics?" is about absorption and achievable concentration at the site of infection. Plenty of admitted patients should be on oral drugs, and a few outpatients genuinely need parenteral therapy.

IV is genuinely requiredWhy
Haemodynamic instability / septic shockSplanchnic hypoperfusion makes enteral absorption unpredictable, and the volume of distribution is deranged.
Cannot swallow, vomiting, ileus, malabsorption, NPO, NG suctionNo absorption, no drug.
Meningitis and other CNS infectionRequires bactericidal CSF concentrations that oral agents cannot reliably produce.
Endocarditis (at least the initial phase)Bacteria in an avascular vegetation need sustained high bactericidal levels.
S. aureus bacteraemiaHigh complication and metastatic-seeding rate; needs source hunting, repeat cultures and ID involvement.
Profound neutropeniaMucositis makes absorption erratic and the consequences of failure are severe.
No adequate oral option exists for the organismE.g. Pseudomonas outside ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin susceptibility; most ESBL and CRE.
Prosthetic material, undrained collection, or uncontrolled sourceThe route is not the problem — the source is. Drain it.
Being on a hospital ward is not, by itself, an indication for intravenous antibiotics. If the patient is stable, improving, and eating, and a bioavailable oral agent covers the organism, the IV line is adding phlebitis, thrombosis and line-infection risk with no benefit. Across the oral-versus-IV literature in stable patients, no randomised trial has shown intravenous administration superior to an equivalent oral agent.
Orders

Admission order set

🧪

What to send before the first dose — and what to trend

Blood cultures ×2Two sets from two separate venipuncture sites, adequate volume (10 mL per bottle), before the first dose. This is what makes de-escalation on day 3 possible. Do not delay antibiotics in septic shock to obtain them.Before abx
Site-specific culturesUrine, sputum or a lower respiratory sample, wound or abscess aspirate, CSF, joint or pleural fluid — whatever matches the suspected source. Aspirate before antibiotics wherever it is safe to do so.Before abx
LactateAt presentation if sepsis is suspected; repeat within 2–4 h if the initial value is >2 mmol/L. A rising lactate on adequate resuscitation means the source is not controlled.Sepsis
CBC with differential, CMP, magnesium, phosphateBaseline renal and hepatic function before dosing; establishes the creatinine you will dose from and the potassium you will watch on TMP-SMX.Admit
Calculate CrClCockcroft-Gault, not the reported eGFR. Every β-lactam dose adjustment, and the cefepime neurotoxicity you are trying to avoid, depends on this number.Admit
MRSA nasal PCROrder it on every patient started on empiric vancomycin for pneumonia. A negative swab has a negative predictive value of about 96.5% overall and 98.1% in community-acquired pneumonia for MRSA pneumonia — it is your licence to stop vancomycin in 24 hours.If on vanc
Procalcitonin (baseline)Only if you intend to trend it and act on the result. A baseline is required for the ≥80%-drop stopping rule to be usable.Optional
Imaging for sourceCXR for respiratory symptoms; CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast for an abdominal source; renal ultrasound or CT for pyelonephritis not improving at 48–72 h (looking for obstruction or abscess); echocardiography for bacteraemia. Undrained source is the commonest cause of "antibiotic failure."Source hunt
Vancomycin level / AUC monitoringOrder pharmacy AUC-guided dosing at initiation. Level at steady state (typically before the 4th dose), creatinine at least twice weekly.If on vanc
Antibiotic stop/review dateWrite the intended duration and a 48–72 h review date in the order at the time you prescribe. An antibiotic without a planned end date will run until someone notices.Every time
Allergy reconciliationDocument what actually happened, when, and whether treatment was required — that is exactly the information PEN-FAST needs. Every admission is a delabelling opportunity.Admit
