Diabetic foot infection (IWGDF/IDSA)

Diabetes changes the microbiology as well as the severity. Acute, previously untreated, mild infection is still mostly gram-positive and can be treated narrowly. Chronic, previously treated, ischaemic, deep or severe infection is polymicrobial — aerobic gram-positives, Enterobacterales and anaerobes together — and needs broader cover. Always probe to bone: a positive probe-to-bone test in a patient with a high pre-test probability substantially raises the likelihood of osteomyelitis and changes the duration from days to weeks.
SeverityRegimenModifiersDuration
Mild — superficial, <2 cm erythema, no systemic signsOral: cephalexin 500 mg QID · amox-clav 875 mg BID · TMP-SMX 1–2 DS BID · doxycycline 100 mg BID · clindamycin 300–450 mg QIDCover MRSA only if prior MRSA, high local prevalence, or severe presentation.1–2 weeks
Moderate — deeper, >2 cm erythema, lymphangitis, fascia/muscle/bone involvement, no systemic toxicityAmpicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV q6h · ertapenem 1 g IV q24h · ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV q24h + metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h · moxifloxacin 400 mg dailyAdd vancomycin for MRSA risk. Add Pseudomonas cover (pip-tazo 4.5 g q6h, cefepime 2 g q8h) for macerated/water-exposed wounds, warm climates, failed therapy, or prior Pseudomonas.1–3 weeks (soft tissue)
Severe — systemic toxicity or metabolic instabilityPiperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h + vancomycin · or meropenem 1 g IV q8h + vancomycinUrgent surgical assessment for debridement, drainage or revascularisation. Vascular studies for ischaemia.2–4 weeks (soft tissue)
Osteomyelitis presentCulture-directed — bone biopsy where possible, not a superficial swabSuperficial swabs correlate poorly with bone culture and lead to wrong therapy.~6 weeks if bone is retained; ~1–3 weeks if all infected bone is resected

Necrotising soft-tissue infection — a surgical emergency

Antibiotics do not treat this disease; the operating room does. Mortality rises with every hour of delay to debridement. Do not let imaging, a score, or a consultant's availability delay surgical consultation. Give antibiotics on the way to theatre.
ComponentDoseWhy
Broad gram-negative + anaerobic backbonePiperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h or meropenem 1 g IV q8hType I (polymicrobial) disease — Enterobacterales, anaerobes, streptococci — is the more common form, especially in diabetics and post-operative patients.
MRSA coverVancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h (or linezolid 600 mg q12h)MRSA is a documented cause of monomicrobial necrotising fasciitis.
Clindamycin900 mg IV q8hAdded regardless of susceptibility for ribosomal toxin suppression in streptococcal and clostridial disease. β-lactams lose potency at high inoculum because organisms are not dividing (the Eagle effect); clindamycin works independent of growth phase. Linezolid can substitute.
AdjunctsRepeat debridement at 12–24 h and until there is no further necrosis. IVIG is sometimes used in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome but the evidence is weak and it must never delay surgery.
The LRINEC score (CRP, WBC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose) was derived to help distinguish necrotising infection from severe cellulitis, but subsequent validation studies found sensitivity too low to rule the diagnosis out. A low LRINEC does not exclude necrotising fasciitis. If the clinical picture fits, operate.
Lobar consolidation. A radiograph is required to diagnose pneumonia — treating a clinical impression alone substantially over-treats viral bronchitis.
Image: X-ray of lobar pneumonia.jpg — Mikael Haggstrom, M.D., CC0 (Wikimedia Commons)
Purulent sputum Gram stain with abundant neutrophils and gram-positive cocci. A good-quality specimen (>25 PMNs and <10 epithelial cells per low-power field) can direct therapy on day one.
Image: Pus in Gram stain showing Gram positive cocci in singles, pairs and clusters.jpg — Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

ATS/IDSA severe CAP = 1 major criterion — mechanical ventilation, or septic shock requiring vasopressors — or ≥3 minor criteria: respiratory rate ≥30/min · PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤250 · multilobar infiltrates · confusion/disorientation · uraemia (BUN ≥20 mg/dL) · leukopenia (WBC <4,000/µL) · thrombocytopenia (platelets <100,000/µL) · hypothermia (<36 °C) · hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation.

Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia (IDSA/ATS 2016)

HAP = pneumonia occurring ≥48 h after admission and not incubating at admission. VAP = pneumonia occurring >48 h after intubation. Cover MSSA, Pseudomonas and other gram-negative bacilli in everyone; add MRSA and a second antipseudomonal agent by risk.

ComponentAgents & dosesWhen to include
Antipseudomonal backbone (always)Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h (extended infusion 4.5 g over 4 h q8h) · cefepime 2 g IV q8h · ceftazidime 2 g IV q8h · meropenem 1 g IV q8h · imipenem 500 mg IV q6h · levofloxacin 750 mg IV dailyAll patients. Note these also cover MSSA.
MRSA coverVancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q8–12h (AUC-guided) or linezolid 600 mg IV q12hIV antibiotics in the last 90 days, ward MRSA prevalence >10–20% (or unknown), prior MRSA isolation, or high mortality risk (ventilatory support or septic shock).
Second antipseudomonal agent (double cover)Add from a different class: tobramycin 5–7 mg/kg IV q24h · amikacin 15–20 mg/kg q24h · ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q8h · levofloxacin 750 mg daily · aztreonam 2 g q8hHigh mortality risk (ventilation or septic shock), IV antibiotics in the last 90 days, structural lung disease, or a unit where >10% of gram-negative isolates are resistant to the chosen monotherapy.
Severe β-lactam allergyAztreonam 2 g IV q8h + vancomycin or linezolid ± an aminoglycosideAztreonam has no gram-positive activity — it always needs a partner.
Seven days is the answer for HAP/VAP — equivalent outcomes to 15 days with less resistance emergence, and the 2016 guideline extends this even to non-fermenting gram-negative rods. Do not use two antipseudomonal agents beyond the point at which susceptibilities return; de-escalate to a single agent.
Aspiration. Most aspiration pneumonia does not need routine anaerobic coverage — ceftriaxone or ampicillin-sulbactam is adequate. Add dedicated anaerobic cover (metronidazole, or use ampicillin-sulbactam/pip-tazo which already have it) only for lung abscess, necrotising pneumonia, empyema, or severe periodontal disease. Aspiration pneumonitis — a chemical injury within hours of a witnessed aspiration, often afebrile with rapid radiographic improvement — needs no antibiotics at all.

Pyelonephritis and complicated UTI — inpatient

ScenarioPreferredAlternative / allergyWhyDuration
Uncomplicated pyelonephritis needing admissionCeftriaxone 1 g IV q24hCiprofloxacin 400 mg IV q12h · gentamicin 5–7 mg/kg IV q24h · ampicillin + gentamicinCovers the great majority of community E. coli; once-daily and no renal adjustment.7 days total (IV then PO); 5 days if switching to levofloxacin 750 mg
Complicated / healthcare-associated / recent antibioticsCefepime 2 g IV q8–12h or piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6hMeropenem 1 g IV q8h if critically ill or prior ESBLAdds Pseudomonas and AmpC cover for the patient with hardware, recent instrumentation, or prior resistant isolates.7–14 days depending on source control
Known or suspected ESBLErtapenem 1 g IV q24h (stable) or meropenem 1 g IV q8h (septic)Aminoglycoside or, for cystitis only, nitrofurantoin/fosfomycinDo not use piperacillin-tazobactam for ESBL bacteraemia — the MERINO trial found 30-day mortality of 12.3% with pip-tazo versus 3.7% with meropenem.7–14 days
Enterococcal or catheter-associatedAmpicillin 2 g IV q4–6h (or vancomycin if resistant/allergic)Linezolid or daptomycin for VRENo cephalosporin covers enterococcus. Remove or exchange the catheter — you cannot treat a biofilm you leave in place.7 days if prompt response; 10–14 if delayed
Pyelonephritis not improving by 48–72 h needs imaging, not a broader antibiotic. You are looking for obstruction, a perinephric or renal abscess, emphysematous pyelonephritis, or a stone. An obstructed infected system is a urological emergency requiring decompression — nephrostomy or stent — and no antibiotic regimen substitutes for it.
Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in the hospital either. A positive urine culture in a patient with delirium and no urinary symptoms is one of the commonest sources of unnecessary inpatient antibiotics. Look for another cause of the delirium first. The exceptions remain pregnancy and pre-urologic-procedure.

Complicated intra-abdominal infection

Every intra-abdominal regimen must cover gram-negative Enterobacterales plus anaerobes. Either use a single agent that does both (pip-tazo, a carbapenem, a cephamycin) or combine a cephalosporin/fluoroquinolone with metronidazole. Adding metronidazole to pip-tazo or a carbapenem is redundant. Source control — drainage, resection, diversion — outranks every antibiotic decision here.
Risk stratumPreferredAlternativeAdd-onsDuration
Community-acquired, mild–moderateCeftriaxone 1–2 g IV q24h + metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h · ertapenem 1 g IV q24hCefoxitin 2 g IV q6h · ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q12h + metronidazole (allergy) · moxifloxacin 400 mg dailyNo routine enterococcal or antifungal cover.4 days after adequate source control (STOP-IT)
High-risk / healthcare-associated / severe physiologic derangementPiperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h · meropenem 1 g IV q8hCefepime 2 g IV q8h + metronidazole 500 mg q8hAdd vancomycin for MRSA risk. Add enterococcal cover (ampicillin, or vancomycin/linezolid) for postoperative, immunocompromised, valvular, or prior-cephalosporin patients. Add an echinocandin for upper-GI perforation, recurrent leak, or Candida on culture.4–7 days after source control
Acute cholangitis (Tokyo Guidelines 2018)Grade I/II: ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV q24h + metronidazole or ertapenem 1 g q24h. Grade III / healthcare-associated: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g q6h or cefepime 2 g q8h ± metronidazole or a carbapenemAztreonam ± metronidazole in severe β-lactam allergy · ciprofloxacin + metronidazole for Grade I–II if susceptibility knownAdd vancomycin for enterococcal cover in Grade III and healthcare-associated disease. Add metronidazole if a biliary-enteric anastomosis is present.4–7 days after source control. If gram-positive cocci (Enterococcus, Streptococcus) are in the blood, extend to a minimum of 2 weeks because of endocarditis risk.
Acute cholecystitis (TG18)As for Grade-matched cholangitis——Grade I–II: antibiotics can be stopped within 24 h of cholecystectomy. Extend to 4–7 days if there is perforation, emphysematous change, or gangrene.
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitisCeftriaxone 2 g IV q24hCefotaxime 2 g IV q8h · pip-tazo if healthcare-associated or recent antibiotic exposureAlbumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 reduces hepatorenal syndrome and mortality. Diagnose on ascitic PMN ≥250/µL.5 days
Timing of biliary drainage in cholangitis. Grade I (mild) usually responds to antibiotics alone — drain if there is no response within 24 h. Grade II (moderate) needs early endoscopic or percutaneous drainage; in the international validation cohort, drainage within 24 h was associated with lower 30-day mortality than later or no drainage (1.7% vs 3.4%). Grade III (severe) needs organ support first, then drainage as soon as the patient can tolerate it.

Bacterial meningitis — the most time-critical antibiotic decision in medicine

Give dexamethasone plus antibiotics immediately. If a CT is needed before LP, draw blood cultures, give dexamethasone and antibiotics first, and do the LP afterwards — CSF cell counts, protein and glucose remain interpretable for hours, and Gram stain and PCR often still yield the organism.
PopulationEmpiric regimen (full CNS doses)Why
Age 1 month–50 years, immunocompetentVancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h + ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12hPneumococcus and meningococcus. Vancomycin is added because CSF pneumococcal breakpoints are far stricter than non-CNS ones — a "susceptible" pneumococcus may still fail ceftriaxone in the CSF.
Age >50, pregnancy, alcohol use disorder, or immunocompromiseAdd ampicillin 2 g IV q4hListeria monocytogenes — intrinsically resistant to every cephalosporin. Missing this is the classic and lethal error.
Post-neurosurgical, penetrating head trauma, CSF shunt/drainVancomycin + cefepime 2 g IV q8h (or meropenem 2 g IV q8h, or ceftazidime 2 g IV q8h)Adds Pseudomonas and nosocomial gram-negatives; staphylococci (including coagulase-negative) are covered by vancomycin. Usually also requires hardware removal.
Severe β-lactam allergyVancomycin + moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily; TMP-SMX 10–20 mg/kg/day of TMP divided q6–12h replaces ampicillin for Listeria; meropenem 2 g q8h is usually toleratedAztreonam covers gram-negatives but nothing else — it needs partners.
Dexamethasone0.15 mg/kg IV q6h for 4 days, first dose 10–20 minutes before or concurrent with the first antibiotic doseReduces unfavourable outcome and mortality, driven by the pneumococcal subgroup. Stop it if the organism turns out not to be pneumococcus. Given after antibiotics it loses benefit — the mechanism is blunting the inflammatory burst caused by bacterial lysis.
OrganismDirected therapyDuration
N. meningitidisCeftriaxone 2 g q12h (or penicillin G 4 MU q4h if susceptible)7 days
H. influenzaeCeftriaxone 2 g q12h7 days
S. pneumoniaeCeftriaxone ± vancomycin by MIC10–14 days
L. monocytogenesAmpicillin 2 g q4h ± gentamicin≥21 days
Aerobic gram-negative bacilliCefepime or meropenem 2 g q8h21 days
CT head before LP is indicated for: immunocompromise, known CNS disease (mass, stroke, focal infection), new-onset seizure within the preceding week, papilloedema, abnormal level of consciousness, or a focal neurological deficit. In everyone else, LP first — and in everyone, antibiotics and steroids first if there is any delay.

Septic arthritis

ScenarioRegimenWhyDuration
Native joint, empiricVancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h ± ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h (or cefepime 2 g q8h if gram-negative/nosocomial risk)S. aureus is the commonest cause; add gram-negative cover for the elderly, immunocompromised, IV drug use, or gram-negative rods on Gram stain.2–4 weeks, guided by organism and response
Suspected gonococcal (young, sexually active, tenosynovitis + dermatitis + migratory polyarthralgia)Ceftriaxone 1 g IV/IM q24h, plus doxycycline 100 mg BID ×7 d for chlamydiaDisseminated gonococcal infection behaves differently — it responds fast and often does not need washout.7 days (at least 24–48 h of clinical improvement before oral step-down)
AlwaysAspirate the joint before antibiotics and send cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals. Synovial WBC >50,000/µL with >90% neutrophils strongly suggests septic arthritis (though lower counts do not exclude it, especially in prosthetic joints and immunocompromise). Drainage — repeated aspiration, arthroscopic or open washout — is part of the treatment, not optional.

Osteomyelitis

ScenarioRegimenDurationKey point
Native, empiric pending cultureVancomycin + ceftriaxone 2 g q24h (or cefepime 2 g q8h)—Whenever the patient is stable, hold antibiotics and get a bone biopsy first. Superficial swabs mislead.
MSSACefazolin 2 g IV q8h or nafcillin 2 g IV q4h6 weeks from the start of definitive therapy (or last debridement)—
MRSAVancomycin (AUC-guided) · daptomycin 6–10 mg/kg q24h · linezolid 600 mg q12h6 weeksLinezolid beyond 4 weeks requires weekly CBC and neuropathy screening.
Vertebral osteomyelitis (IDSA 2015)Culture-directed after image-guided biopsy6 weeksGet an MRI. Follow ESR/CRP. Urgent surgery for cord compression, epidural abscess with deficit, or instability.
Prosthetic joint infectionCulture-directed IV, plus rifampin 300–450 mg PO BID for staphylococcal infection with retained hardwareTypically 2–6 weeks IV then prolonged oral suppression, per surgical strategyRifampin penetrates biofilm but must never be given alone. Surgical strategy — debridement with implant retention versus one- or two-stage exchange — drives the whole plan.
Oral therapy works for bone and joint infection. The OVIVA trial randomised 1,054 patients to oral versus IV therapy for the first 6 weeks of bone and joint infection and found oral non-inferior (treatment failure 13.2% oral vs 14.6% IV), with far fewer catheter complications (1.0% vs 9.4%) and a shorter stay. This was ID-supervised with highly bioavailable oral regimens — it is a specialist decision, not a reflexive floor switch, but it has ended the automatic "6 weeks of IV" reflex.

Infective endocarditis

ScenarioRegimenDurationWhy
Native valve, empiric (acutely ill, awaiting cultures)Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h + ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24hUntil cultures direct therapyCovers staphylococci (including MRSA), streptococci and the HACEK organisms. Send three sets of blood cultures from separate sites before starting.
MSSA, native valveNafcillin or oxacillin 12 g/24 h IV divided q4–6h, or cefazolin 2 g IV q8h6 weeksCefazolin is equivalent with better tolerability. Do not use vancomycin for MSSA.
MRSA, native valveVancomycin (AUC-guided) or daptomycin ≥8 mg/kg IV q24h6 weeksHigher daptomycin doses are used in endocarditis than the 6 mg/kg label dose. Weekly CPK.
Viridans strep / S. gallolyticus, highly penicillin-susceptiblePenicillin G 12–18 MU/24 h IV (continuous or divided q4–6h) or ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h4 weeks; 2 weeks if combined with gentamicin 3 mg/kg q24h in uncomplicated native-valve diseaseS. gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis) endocarditis mandates a colonoscopy — it is strongly associated with colonic neoplasia.
EnterococcusAmpicillin 2 g IV q4h + ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h6 weeksThe double-β-lactam regimen saturates complementary PBPs and has replaced ampicillin + gentamicin — equal efficacy, far less nephrotoxicity, and it works against high-level-gentamicin-resistant strains.
Prosthetic valve, staphylococcalVancomycin (or nafcillin if MSSA) + rifampin 300 mg IV/PO q8h + gentamicin 3 mg/kg/24 h≥6 weeks (gentamicin for the first 2 weeks)Rifampin for biofilm on the prosthetic material — added only after bacteraemia has cleared, and never alone.
Surgical indications — do not delay the surgical conversation: heart failure from valvular dysfunction; uncontrolled infection (abscess, fistula, enlarging vegetation on therapy); persistent bacteraemia beyond 5–7 days of appropriate therapy; prosthetic valve endocarditis; fungal or highly resistant organisms; recurrent emboli or a large mobile vegetation (>10 mm) with prior embolism.
POET randomised 400 patients with stabilised left-sided endocarditis, after at least 10 days of IV therapy, to partial oral versus continued IV therapy and found the oral strategy non-inferior (composite event 9.0% vs 12.1%), with post-randomisation stay of 3 days versus 19. It is an ID-directed decision in a highly selected, stabilised patient — not a routine floor manoeuvre.
Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia is never a "contaminant" and never a short course. Every case needs: repeat blood cultures every 48–72 h until clearance, echocardiography (TOE if prosthetic material, persistent bacteraemia, or a high-risk picture), a source hunt for metastatic foci, removal of any infected line, and ID consultation — which is independently associated with lower mortality. Minimum 14 days from the first negative culture for genuinely uncomplicated disease; 4–6 weeks if complicated.
Switch

IV → PO conversion

🔄

The highest-yield stewardship intervention on the ward

Switching to oral therapy is not a downgrade — for a stable patient with a bioavailable oral option it is the better treatment, because it removes a line. Every intravenous day carries phlebitis, thrombosis and bloodstream-infection risk that the oral route simply does not have. In the OVIVA trial of bone and joint infection, catheter complications occurred in 9.4% of the IV arm versus 1.0% of the oral arm — a number needed to treat of 12 to prevent one line complication, with no loss of efficacy.

The switch criteria — all must be satisfied

CriterionThresholdWhy
Haemodynamically stableNo vasopressors; blood pressure and heart rate stable without fluid bolusesShock deranges splanchnic perfusion and the volume of distribution — absorption becomes unpredictable.
AfebrileTemperature <38 °C for at least 24 hours (older protocols required 48 h or two consecutive readings)A health system that relaxed its trigger from 48 h to 24 h raised oral conversion from 38% to 64% and cut median length of stay from 4 days to 2.5 days with no change in readmission or mortality.
White count improvingTrending down and <20,000/µL; many modern protocols have dropped this criterion entirelyA single WBC value is a poor marker; the trend matters.
Clinically improvingSymptoms of the index infection resolving; no new deteriorationThe core judgement — everything else is a proxy.
Functioning gutEating or tolerating tube feeds; no vomiting, ileus, short-bowel syndrome, severe diarrhoea, NPO status, NG suction, or documented malabsorptionActive vomiting is a hard exclusion in every published protocol.
An adequate oral agent existsSufficient bioavailability and spectrum for this organism at this siteIf there is no oral drug that covers the bug at that site, there is no switch to make — this is the criterion most often skipped.
Syndromes where IV continues regardless of how well the patient looks: bacterial meningitis and other CNS infection · infective endocarditis (the POET trial's partial-oral strategy applies only to stabilised left-sided disease after ≥10 days of IV therapy, and is an ID decision) · S. aureus bacteraemia (the SABATO trial found oral step-down non-inferior, but only 4.2% of screened patients were eligible — this is not a floor decision) · profound neutropenia with mucositis · an undrained abscess or otherwise uncontrolled source · infected prosthetic material · severe sepsis or septic shock.

TMP-SMXTMP ~98–102%, SMX ~86–99%1 : 1 (mg/kg)Studied in critically ill patients: no dose adjustment needed when switching routes.
RifampinNot stated on the label1 : 1IV doses are the same as oral — but give the oral dose on an empty stomach (food reduces absorption ~30%).
Clindamycin~90%Not by doseAbsorption is excellent; the problem is a dose ceiling — the labeled oral maximum is 450 mg q6h (1,800 mg/day) versus up to 2,700 mg/day IV. IV 600–900 mg q8h maps to about 450 mg PO q8h.
Ciprofloxacin~70%Dose must riseIV 400 mg q12h → PO 500 mg q12h; IV 400 mg q8h → PO 750 mg q12h.
Azithromycin~38%1 : 1 in practiceSerum bioavailability is low but tissue concentrations are what matter; the label's own CAP regimen switches IV 500 mg to PO 500 mg.
Cefuroxime axetil37% fasting → 52% with foodNoMust be given with food — a patient told to take it on an empty stomach is being under-dosed by a third.
Cefpodoxime~50% fasting (AUC 21–33% higher with food)NoAlso give with food. Blocked by antacids and PPIs.
Cefdinir21% at 300 mg · 16% at 600 mgNoLow and saturable — a bigger dose does not fix it (absorption is less than dose-proportional). Peak concentrations are ~1.6–2.3 mg/L versus 15–18 mg/L for cephalexin. A poor step-down for bacteraemia.

Specific IV → PO conversions

IV regimenOral step-downCaveat
Levofloxacin 750 mg IV dailyLevofloxacin 750 mg PO dailyTruly interchangeable. Hold tube feeds and cation-containing products around the dose.
Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q8hCiprofloxacin 750 mg PO q12hThe only oral antipseudomonal option, alongside levofloxacin.
Metronidazole 500 mg IV q8hMetronidazole 500 mg PO q8hSwitch on day 1 in any patient who can swallow.
Linezolid 600 mg IV q12hLinezolid 600 mg PO q12hVerify insurance coverage — cost is the usual barrier, not pharmacology.
Azithromycin 500 mg IV dailyAzithromycin 500 mg PO dailyThe label's own CAP regimen: ≥2 IV days then oral to complete 7–10 days.
Clindamycin 600–900 mg IV q8hClindamycin 450 mg PO q8h (up to 600 mg q8h for severe MRSA at some institutions)Take with a full glass of water, sitting up — pill oesophagitis is common.
Ampicillin IVAmoxicillin 1,000 mg PO TIDOral ampicillin itself is a poor choice — bioavailability only 30–55% and food-sensitive.
Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV q6hAmoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID (consider TID if BMI ≥30)Do not build a 1 g dose from two 500/125 tablets — the clavulanate load causes diarrhoea.
Cefazolin 1–2 g IV q8hCephalexin 500 mg PO QID (1 g PO q12h is restricted to cystitis at some centres)Cephalexin's gram-negative coverage is weaker than cefazolin's — for anything beyond skin or cystitis, choose by the isolate's susceptibilities.
Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV q24hNo single oral equivalent. By susceptibility: cefpodoxime 200–400 mg PO BID · cefuroxime axetil 500 mg PO BID · amox-clav 875 mg PO BID · cephalexin 500 mg PO QID · or (often better) a fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMXYou cannot reliably infer oral third-generation cephalosporin susceptibility from a ceftriaxone-susceptible result. Cefdinir's low bioavailability makes it a poor choice for bacteraemia; for urinary sources, penetration ranks cefuroxime > cefpodoxime > cefdinir.
Nafcillin / oxacillin IVAnti-staphylococcal oral step-down — institution-specific and ID-directedDicloxacillin 500 mg PO QID is the dose in the IDSA skin-infection guideline but exceeds the package-insert maximum; cephalexin is more commonly used in practice. Never step down S. aureus bacteraemia without ID input.
Piperacillin-tazobactam · cefepime · meropenem · ertapenemNo oral equivalent exists. Step down by susceptibility — a fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX is the usual carbapenem-sparing option for ESBL EnterobacteralesThere is no oral antipseudomonal agent other than ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin, and no oral carbapenem at all.
Vancomycin IVLinezolid 600 mg PO BID · TMP-SMX · doxycycline, by susceptibility and siteOral vancomycin is not a step-down for anything systemic — it is not absorbed and treats only C. difficile.

The preference order for oral step-down of Enterobacterales bacteraemia

  1. Ciprofloxacin 750 mg PO BID or levofloxacin 750 mg PO daily — highest and most reliable exposure.
  2. TMP-SMX 8–10 mg/kg/day of the trimethoprim component divided BID–TID (roughly 1 DS BID at 40–59 kg, 1 DS TID at 60–69 kg, 2 DS BID at 70–89 kg).
  3. β-lactams — cefuroxime 500 mg BID, amoxicillin 1,000 mg TID, cephalexin 500 mg QID, amox-clav 875 mg BID. Avoid entirely in ESBL or AmpC producers.
Monitor

Daily rounds & de-escalation

📈

The 48–72 hour antibiotic time-out

By 48–72 hours you have culture data, a clinical trajectory and a diagnosis you either believe or don't. This is the moment when broad empiric therapy either becomes targeted therapy or becomes an ongoing harm. Build the time-out into your daily note.

Empiric therapy is a hypothesis with a 48–72 hour expiry. If nothing changes at the time-out, the default is that the broadest possible regimen runs to completion — which is how resistance and C. difficile happen.

What to trend daily

ParameterWhat good looks likeWhat a bad answer means
Temperature and heart rateDefervescence by 48–72 hPersistent fever = undrained source, resistant organism, wrong diagnosis, drug fever, or a line infection.
White count, lactateFallingA rising lactate on adequate fluid resuscitation is a source-control problem until proven otherwise.
Creatinine and potassiumStableVancomycin/aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity; TMP-SMX hyperkalaemia; consider dose adjustment.
Repeat blood culturesClearedMandatory in S. aureus, candidaemia and endocarditis — repeat every 48–72 h until negative. Persistent bacteraemia means a deep focus.
Vancomycin AUC / levelAUC₂₄ 400–600Above 600 adds nephrotoxicity without efficacy; below 400 risks failure.
Exam of the sourceErythema border receding, drain output falling, wound granulatingRe-image. The commonest reason antibiotics "fail" is that the source was never controlled.
Lines and devicesRemoved as soon as not neededEvery retained line is a nidus. Remove the central line in S. aureus, Candida, Pseudomonas or persistent bacteraemia.

De-escalation — the specific moves

SituationMove
MRSA nasal PCR negative in pneumoniaStop vancomycin/linezolid. Negative predictive value ~96.5% overall and ~98.1% in community-acquired pneumonia. This alone saves an average of about a day of unnecessary vancomycin per patient.
Culture grows MSSAStop vancomycin; start cefazolin 2 g q8h or nafcillin 2 g q4h. Vancomycin is inferior for MSSA.
Cultures negative at 48–72 h in a patient who has improvedStop the empiric MRSA and antipseudomonal agents. Negative cultures in an improving patient are permission to narrow.
On pip-tazo or a carbapenem plus metronidazoleStop the metronidazole — the anaerobic coverage is already there. Redundant coverage is pure added toxicity.
Coagulase-negative staph in 1 of 4 bottles, patient well, no hardwareContaminant. Do not treat. Repeat cultures if genuinely uncertain.
Positive urine culture, no urinary symptomsAsymptomatic bacteriuria. Do not treat (except pregnancy or pre-urologic procedure). Look elsewhere for the cause of the delirium.
Sputum or wound culture growing an organism in a patient with no clinical infectionColonisation. Do not treat. Treat the patient, not the culture.
Two antipseudomonal agents, susceptibilities now backDrop to a single agent. Double coverage is for the empiric window only.
Stable, afebrile 24 h, eating, oral option existsSwitch to oral and plan discharge.
The harms are real and quantified. Roughly one in five hospitalised patients receiving antibiotics experiences an antibiotic-associated adverse event, and about one in five of those occurs in a patient whose antibiotic was not clinically indicated — an entirely avoidable harm. Add C. difficile, resistance selection, and an allergy label that will steer that patient toward worse antibiotics for the rest of their life. "Just in case" is not a benign default.
Escalate

When to broaden or call ICU

⬆️

Numeric triggers

Transfer to ICU for any of: vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP ≥65 after ≥30 mL/kg crystalloid · lactate >4 mmol/L, or failing to clear on adequate resuscitation · need for mechanical ventilation, or PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤250 with rising oxygen requirement · respiratory rate ≥30 with accessory muscle use or a rising PaCO₂ · GCS drop or new focal deficit · urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for >2 h despite fluids · arrhythmia with haemodynamic compromise · ≥3 ATS/IDSA minor severe-CAP criteria · any patient needing hourly nursing reassessment.
Trigger to broaden antibioticsWhat to add
Clinical deterioration on appropriate therapy with a controlled sourceConsider resistant gram-negatives — escalate to cefepime or a carbapenem; add MRSA cover if not already present.
Prior ESBL or CRE isolate anywhere in the last 12 monthsCarbapenem for ESBL; ceftazidime-avibactam or meropenem-vaborbactam for KPC-type CRE; involve ID.
New hypotension or lactate riseBroaden and re-image for source control. Broadening without re-imaging is the classic error.
Neutropenia developsAntipseudomonal β-lactam immediately; add vancomycin only for the specific indications.
Fungal risk — TPN, prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics, upper-GI perforation, Candida on culture from a sterile siteEchinocandin (e.g. micafungin 100 mg IV daily); remove central lines in candidaemia; ophthalmology exam.
Before you broaden, ask whether the problem is really the antibiotic. The differential for "not improving on antibiotics" is: undrained collection · retained infected hardware or line · wrong organism (fungal, mycobacterial, viral) · wrong diagnosis entirely (PE, drug fever, malignancy, crystal arthropathy, vasculitis, DVT masquerading as cellulitis) · inadequate dosing for the site or body size · malabsorption on an oral agent. Broadening fixes only one of those.
Dispo

Discharge, OPAT & disposition

🏠

Discharge readiness & where they go

Clinical stability (Halm criteria) — validated in pneumonia and a sound general framework: temperature ≤37.8 °C · heart rate ≤100 · respiratory rate ≤24 · systolic BP ≥90 mmHg · SaO₂ ≥90% or PaO₂ ≥60 mmHg on room air · able to take oral intake · normal mental status (or back to baseline).

Do not discharge on an abnormal vital sign because "they look fine." In a cohort of 3,984 pneumonia patients, 20.4% were discharged with at least one instability in the preceding 24 hours, and that was associated with an adjusted odds ratio of 3.70 for 30-day mortality. Notably, readmission was not significantly increased — these patients die rather than come back. Hypotension (aOR 4.51) and tachypnoea (aOR 3.13) were the strongest individual predictors. Conversely, once stability is achieved, subsequent deterioration requiring escalation occurs in ≤1% of cases.

Also required before discharge

  • Source control documented — the drain placed, the stone removed, the line pulled, the collection evacuated. Write it in the discharge summary.
  • A specific stop date on the prescription, not "until finished."
  • The patient can obtain and afford the drug. Linezolid, fidaxomicin and the newer agents can be prohibitively expensive — verify coverage before discharge, because an unfilled prescription is worse than an extra inpatient day.
  • Adherence-friendly dosing. Cefpodoxime BID beats cephalexin QID for a patient who will struggle with four doses a day; prefer the least frequent effective regimen.
  • Follow-up booked before the course ends, with explicit return precautions.
  • Allergy label reviewed — this admission is a delabelling opportunity.

OPAT — outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy

ElementDetail
WhoA stable patient needing prolonged parenteral therapy — endocarditis, osteomyelitis, complicated bacteraemia, CNS infection, resistant organisms with no oral option. Patients or caregivers may self-administer, with comparable safety to nurse-administered therapy. For people who inject drugs, the IDSA guideline makes no blanket exclusion — it is explicitly a case-by-case decision.
AccessPICC or tunnelled line for courses beyond ~2 weeks; a midline may suffice for shorter courses and non-vesicant drugs. Every line is a bloodstream-infection risk that must be justified.
MonitoringWeekly CBC and CMP as a baseline standard. Add vancomycin levels (AUC-guided), weekly CPK for daptomycin, LFTs for prolonged β-lactams and rifampin, and CBC weekly for linezolid and ceftaroline. A named physician must be responsible for reviewing the results.
Line-free alternatives — always ask firstDalbavancin 1500 mg IV ×1 or oritavancin 1200 mg IV ×1 for gram-positive SSTI — a single infusion and no line at all. Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily or ertapenem 1 g IV daily for once-daily home therapy. Or an oral regimen — OVIVA for bone and joint infection and POET for stabilised endocarditis both showed oral non-inferiority in selected patients. The best line is no line.

Home

Stable, oral regimen, can self-manage, reliable follow-up within 48–72 h.

Home health

Home plus nursing for wound care, IV administration, or line management.

SNF

Needs 24-hour skilled nursing — complex wound care, IV therapy without home support, or deconditioning with <3 h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Can tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines — e.g. after debridement, amputation, or post-meningitis deficits.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care >25 days — ventilator weaning, extensive wounds, multi-week IV therapy with instability.

Hospice / palliative

Recurrent infection in advanced illness. Antibiotics are a legitimate comfort measure in some cases (dysuria, purulent secretions) and a burden in others — decide by goals, not reflex.
🫀 ICU — broad-spectrum therapy, MDRO coverage, source control & de-escalation
Admit

Sepsis & the antibiotic clock

🚨

How fast, and how broad

Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection — operationally, an acute rise in the SOFA score of ≥2 points attributable to infection. Septic shock is sepsis with vasopressor requirement to keep MAP ≥65 mmHg and a lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate volume resuscitation, and carries hospital mortality above 40%.

Clinical situationAntibiotic timing (Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Septic shock, or sepsis with a high likelihood of infectionImmediately — ideally within 1 hour of recognition
Possible sepsis without shockRapid focused assessment for infectious versus non-infectious cause; if concern persists, antimicrobials within 3 hours of first recognition
Low likelihood of infection, no shockDefer antimicrobials while continuing to monitor closely and search for the cause
In septic shock, mortality rises measurably with every hour of delay to effective antimicrobial therapy. Draw two sets of blood cultures if it can be done in minutes — but never let culture collection delay the first dose in a patient in shock. Give the antibiotic, then keep looking for the source.

The first hour, alongside antibiotics

  • Fluids: at least 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid within 3 hours for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock, then reassess with dynamic measures rather than giving fixed further boluses.
  • Lactate: measure at presentation and remeasure within 2–4 h if elevated. A lactate that fails to clear on adequate resuscitation is a source-control problem.
  • Vasopressors: start norepinephrine for MAP ≥65 mmHg — peripherally if needed rather than waiting for central access.
  • Source control: identify and act on a drainable or removable source as soon as medically and logistically practical. This is the intervention with the largest effect size in the entire bundle.
AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeEffectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα₁ ≫ β₁0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min (higher in refractory shock)↑↑SVR, modest ↑CO, little tachycardiaFirst-line in septic shock. Start peripherally rather than delay for a central line.
VasopressinV₁ receptor — a non-catecholamine pathwayFixed 0.03 units/min (not titrated)↑SVR; catecholamine-sparingAdd when norepinephrine reaches roughly 0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min, to limit catecholamine dose.
Epinephrineα₁, β₁, β₂0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑CO and ↑SVRThird agent, or when there is coexisting myocardial depression. Raises lactate through β₂-driven glycolysis — do not misread this as worsening perfusion.
Dobutamineβ₁ > β₂2.5–20 mcg/kg/min↑contractility, ↑CO, may ↓SVRSepsis-induced cardiomyopathy with persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate volume and MAP.
HydrocortisoneRestores vascular catecholamine responsiveness200 mg/day (50 mg IV q6h or continuous infusion)Faster shock reversalOngoing vasopressor requirement — typically norepinephrine ≥0.25 mcg/kg/min for ≥4 hours.
Septic shock is distributive — profound α-mediated vasodilation with a normal or high cardiac output. That is why the first drug is an α₁ agonist and not an inotrope, and why giving an inotrope to a vasodilated patient makes the blood pressure worse.
Treat

Broad-spectrum & MDRO coverage

🛡️

Which holes to plug, and the evidence for plugging them

Empiric ICU therapy is built by asking the three-holes question — MRSA? Pseudomonas? anaerobes? — and then adding a fourth for the patient with resistance history: ESBL or CRE? Each addition must be justified by a risk factor, because each one carries cost. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign explicitly recommends against empiric MRSA coverage in patients at low risk, and against routine double gram-negative coverage in patients at low risk of multidrug resistance.

HoleCover it when…Agent & doseThen stop it when…
MRSAKnown MRSA colonisation or prior infection · IV antibiotics in the last 90 days · haemodialysis · injection drug use · indwelling vascular device · necrotising or purulent SSTI · post-influenza pneumonia · high local prevalence · septic shock with an unclear sourceVancomycin load 20–35 mg/kg TBW (max 3 g) then 15–20 mg/kg q8–12h, AUC 400–600 · linezolid 600 mg IV q12h (preferred for pneumonia — better lung penetration) · daptomycin 6–10 mg/kg (never for pneumonia) · ceftaroline 600 mg q12hNasal MRSA PCR negative in pneumonia (NPV ~96.5% overall, ~98.1% in CAP), or cultures negative at 48–72 h in an improving patient.
PseudomonasStructural lung disease (bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, advanced COPD) · neutropenia · prior Pseudomonas isolation · recent broad-spectrum antibiotics or hospitalisation · ventilator · burns · indwelling devices · severe immunosuppressionCefepime 2 g IV q8h · pip-tazo 4.5 g IV q6h (or extended infusion 4.5 g over 4 h q8h) · meropenem 1–2 g IV q8h · ceftazidime 2 g q8h · ceftolozane-tazobactam 3 g q8h for MDRCultures return a susceptible non-Pseudomonal organism, or cultures are negative at 48–72 h.
AnaerobesIntra-abdominal source · aspiration with lung abscess, empyema or necrotising pneumonia · necrotising SSTI · odontogenic or deep neck source · perirectal diseaseMetronidazole 500 mg IV q8h added to a cephalosporin or fluoroquinolone — or use a backbone that already covers anaerobes: pip-tazo, a carbapenem, ampicillin-sulbactam, cefoxitinImmediately, if the backbone already covers anaerobes. Redundant anaerobic coverage is one of the most common stewardship targets on any ICU list.
ESBLPrior ESBL isolate (any site, last 12 months) · recent β-lactam or fluoroquinolone exposure · long-term care residence · travel to a high-prevalence region · recurrent urinary infection with instrumentationMeropenem 1 g IV q8h (critically ill) · ertapenem 1 g IV q24h (stable). For non-bacteraemic cystitis only: nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin, or an aminoglycosideSusceptibilities allow a narrower agent. Note that IDSA discourages carbapenems for ESBL cystitis when nitrofurantoin or TMP-SMX will do — carbapenem use is the dominant driver of CRE.
CREPrior CRE · prolonged carbapenem exposure · high-prevalence unit · failure on a carbapenemMechanism-directed, with ID: KPC → ceftazidime-avibactam 2.5 g q8h or meropenem-vaborbactam 4 g q8h · metallo-β-lactamase (NDM/VIM/IMP) → cefiderocol 2 g q8h, or ceftazidime-avibactam plus aztreonam · OXA-48 → ceftazidime-avibactamNever de-escalate CRE therapy without ID. Ceftazidime-avibactam and meropenem-vaborbactam do not cover metallo-β-lactamases — identify the enzyme.
CandidaUpper-GI perforation · recurrent anastomotic leak · prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics · TPN · Candida from a sterile site · severe immunosuppression · candidaemia risk with a central lineEchinocandin — e.g. micafungin 100 mg IV daily or caspofungin 70 mg load then 50 mg daily. Step down to fluconazole when the isolate is susceptible and the patient is stableRemove the central line in candidaemia, get a dilated ophthalmology exam, and repeat blood cultures to document clearance.
Should I double-cover Pseudomonas? Empiric double coverage — two antipseudomonal agents from different classes — is justified only while you are waiting for susceptibilities in a patient with septic shock plus a genuine risk of multidrug resistance, or on a unit where more than about 10% of gram-negative isolates would be resistant to your chosen monotherapy. It is a hedge against picking the wrong empiric drug, not a synergy strategy: once susceptibilities return, drop to a single agent. Continuing double coverage adds nephrotoxicity and resistance without benefit.
The vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam AKI story is a lesson in evidence quality. A large body of observational data suggested this combination roughly tripled AKI risk, and it changed practice across the country. The randomised ACORN trial then compared pip-tazo with cefepime in patients also receiving vancomycin and found no difference in kidney injury — while cefepime looked worse neurologically. The likely explanation for the observational signal is that piperacillin-tazobactam interferes with creatinine secretion, producing a rise in measured creatinine without true injury. Dose vancomycin by AUC, watch the creatinine, and do not choose your gram-negative agent on the basis of the old signal alone.
Dosing

PK/PD in critical illness

⚗️

Why the ward dose is often the wrong ICU dose

Critical illness distorts almost every pharmacokinetic parameter at once. Capillary leak and aggressive fluid resuscitation expand the volume of distribution of hydrophilic drugs — β-lactams, vancomycin, aminoglycosides — so standard doses produce sub-therapeutic concentrations exactly when you can least afford them. Hypoalbuminaemia raises the free fraction of highly protein-bound drugs like ceftriaxone and increases their clearance. And a subgroup of patients develops augmented renal clearance — a CrCl above roughly 130 mL/min, classically in younger patients with sepsis, trauma or burns and no pre-existing renal disease — who clear renally eliminated antibiotics so fast that normal dosing fails.

Loading dose
Never reduce
Driven by volume of distribution, not clearance — give the full load even in anuria or on CRRT
β-lactam target
100% fT>MIC
Higher than the 40–70% used in non-critical illness
Vancomycin
AUC 400–600
Bayesian estimation; achieve the target within 24–48 h
Augmented clearance
CrCl >130
Young, trauma/sepsis, normal baseline renal function → under-dosing risk
StrategyHowWhy it works
Extended-infusion β-lactamsPiperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g over 4 hours q8h; meropenem 1–2 g over 3 hours q8h; cefepime 2 g over 3 hours q8hβ-lactam killing is time-dependent. Prolonging the infusion raises the fraction of the interval spent above the MIC far more effectively than raising the dose — the single most useful PK manoeuvre in the ICU, and increasingly the default for critically ill patients and less-susceptible organisms.
Front-loadingFull loading doses of vancomycin (20–35 mg/kg TBW, max 3 g), colistin and aminoglycosides regardless of renal functionThe loading dose fills an expanded volume of distribution. Reducing it for renal failure is a common and dangerous error — renal function governs the maintenance dose, not the load.
Weight-based dosing done properlyVancomycin on total body weight; aminoglycosides on adjusted body weight; cefazolin 2–3 g rather than 1 g in obesityUnder-dosing the obese critically ill patient is routine and consequential.
Recognise augmented renal clearanceMeasure a urinary creatinine clearance rather than trusting an estimating equation in a young patient with a low serum creatinineAn estimating equation cannot detect hyperfiltration. These patients need shortened intervals or extended infusions.
Dose for the organ-support modalityCRRT clears drug continuously — many agents need higher doses than intermittent haemodialysis would suggest. ECMO circuits sequester lipophilic and highly protein-bound drugs"Renal failure, so halve the dose" is wrong on CRRT and causes treatment failure. Involve ICU pharmacy for every patient on an extracorporeal circuit.
Therapeutic drug monitoring where availableVancomycin AUC; aminoglycoside peaks and troughs; β-lactam levels where offeredThe only way to know you have hit the target in a patient whose physiology is changing daily.
Cefepime neurotoxicity is an ICU disease. Encephalopathy, myoclonus, and non-convulsive status epilepticus occur when cefepime accumulates — typically in renal impairment with an unadjusted dose, in the elderly, or when a patient's renal function falls mid-course and nobody re-doses. The presentation looks exactly like ICU delirium, so it is routinely treated with antipsychotics instead of being recognised. If a patient on cefepime develops unexplained encephalopathy or myoclonus, stop the drug and get an EEG. Re-check renal dosing on every ICU patient every day.
Source

Source control

🔧

The intervention that outperforms every antibiotic decision

Antibiotics reach bacteria through blood. A walled-off collection has no blood supply, an abscess interior is acidic and hypoxic (which specifically inactivates aminoglycosides), the bacterial inoculum is enormous and largely non-dividing (which specifically defeats β-lactams), and biofilm on hardware is phenotypically tolerant to nearly everything. No antibiotic regimen substitutes for drainage. If a patient is not improving, the question is almost never "which broader antibiotic?" — it is "what have I not drained?"

SourceControl measureTiming
Intra-abdominal abscess or perforationPercutaneous drainage or laparotomy; diversion if neededAs soon as medically and logistically practical — generally within 6–12 h of recognition
Obstructed infected urinary tractNephrostomy or ureteric stentEmergent — this is a urological emergency
Ascending cholangitisERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction, or percutaneous transhepatic drainageUrgent in moderate disease; after stabilisation in severe disease
Necrotising soft-tissue infectionRadical surgical debridement, repeated at 12–24 h until no further necrosisImmediate — mortality rises with every hour of delay
EmpyemaChest tube ± intrapleural fibrinolytics (alteplase + dornase) or VATS decorticationEarly — a loculated empyema will not resolve on antibiotics
Infected central line or dialysis catheterRemove it for S. aureus, Candida, Pseudomonas, persistent bacteraemia, or tunnel infectionImmediately
Infected prosthesis or hardwareDebridement with retention, or one- or two-stage exchange; rifampin adjunct for staphylococci with retained materialSurgical strategy dictates the whole antibiotic plan
Septic arthritisRepeated aspiration, arthroscopic or open washoutUrgent
Infected pressure ulcer or diabetic footDebridement; revascularisation for ischaemia; amputation where neededEarly surgical and vascular assessment
C. difficile, fulminant with toxic megacolonSubtotal colectomy or diverting loop ileostomy with colonic lavageEarly surgical consultation — do not wait for perforation
Neutropenia

Febrile neutropenia

🧬

Fever may be the only sign there is

Definition: absolute neutrophil count <500 cells/µL — or <1,000/µL with an expected decline to below 500 within 48 hours — plus a single oral temperature ≥38.3 °C, or a temperature ≥38.0 °C sustained over one hour. Without neutrophils there is no pus, no infiltrate, and often no localising sign at all: fever alone is the emergency.

Antibiotics within one hour. Do not wait for imaging, a source, or the culture result. Draw blood cultures from a peripheral site and from every lumen of any central line, then give an antipseudomonal β-lactam immediately.
ComponentRegimenNotes
Inpatient monotherapyCefepime 2 g IV q8h · piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h · meropenem 1 g IV q8h · imipenem-cilastatin 500 mg IV q6hMonotherapy with an antipseudomonal β-lactam is the standard. Ceftriaxone and ertapenem are inadequate — neither covers Pseudomonas.
Add vancomycin only forVancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12hHaemodynamic instability · pneumonia · gram-positive cocci in blood pending identification · clinically suspected catheter-related infection · skin or soft-tissue infection · known MRSA colonisation · severe mucositis. Not routine — adding it empirically to everyone does not improve outcomes, and it should be stopped at 48–72 h if cultures do not support it.
Severe β-lactam allergyAztreonam 2 g IV q6–8h + vancomycin, or ciprofloxacin + vancomycinAztreonam covers no gram-positives — it always needs a partner.
Persistent fever at 4–7 daysAdd empiric antifungal cover — an echinocandin or a mould-active azole; obtain CT chest/sinuses and fungal markersThink invasive aspergillosis in prolonged neutropenia; think Candida with a line or gut translocation.
Low-risk outpatient oral optionCiprofloxacin 750 mg PO BID + amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg PO BIDOnly for carefully selected low-risk patients (MASCC ≥21) with reliable follow-up, no significant comorbidity, no mucositis, and the ability to return quickly. Not if the patient received a fluoroquinolone as prophylaxis.
🧮

MASCC risk index — is this patient low risk?

Higher scores mean lower risk. Maximum 26 points. Score ≥21 identifies low risk — a candidate for oral and/or outpatient management. The burden-of-illness tiers are mutually exclusive and are not additive.

Burden of illness (pick one)
No or mild symptoms +5
Moderate symptoms +3
Severe symptoms / moribund 0
Other factors
No hypotension (SBP >90) +5
No COPD +4
Solid tumour, or haematologic malignancy with no previous fungal infection +4
No dehydration requiring parenteral fluids +3
Outpatient at onset of fever +3
Age <60 years +2
26
MASCC answers "is this patient low risk?" — it is not a severity score, and a high score never overrides a clinician who thinks the patient looks unwell. For seemingly stable solid-tumour outpatients specifically, the CISNE score discriminates better than MASCC and is the more appropriate tool.
Downgrade

De-escalation & transfer out

⬇️

Getting off the broad-spectrum regimen and out of the unit

Antibiotic de-escalation in the ICU

  • Reassess every day, and formally at 48–72 hours. De-escalation in the ICU is safe and is not associated with worse outcomes.
  • Narrow to the isolate the moment susceptibilities return — including switching off vancomycin to cefazolin or nafcillin for MSSA.
  • Stop the empiric MRSA agent if the nasal PCR is negative in pneumonia or cultures are negative at 48–72 h in an improving patient.
  • Drop double gram-negative coverage to a single agent once susceptibilities are known.
  • Stop redundant anaerobic coverage — metronidazole alongside pip-tazo, a carbapenem or a cephamycin.
  • Use procalcitonin with clinical criteria, not alone, to support discontinuation: stop when PCT falls below 0.25 ng/mL or has dropped by ≥80% from peak. Note that this only shortens courses if the team actually acts on it.
  • Fix the stop date. Seven days for HAP/VAP; 4 days after source control for intra-abdominal infection; 7 days for uncomplicated gram-negative bacteraemia. Longer courses do not prevent relapse.

ICU → floor transfer criteria

DomainReady to downgrade
HaemodynamicsOff vasopressors — or on a single low, stable, weaning dose — for ≥6–12 hours, with MAP ≥65 mmHg and no escalation
PerfusionLactate normalised or clearly clearing; urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/h; warm, mentating, creatinine stable or improving
RespiratoryExtubated and stable for several hours (or off non-invasive ventilation) on modest oxygen, with normal respiratory rate and work of breathing
SourceSource controlled — collection drained, line removed, obstruction relieved — with drain output falling and no plan for imminent re-operation
AntibioticsOn a defined regimen with a stop date, no ongoing broadening, and blood cultures cleared where they were positive
MetabolicNo requirement for continuous renal replacement therapy or hourly electrolyte correction
Not yet if: the patient still needs frequent vasopressor titration · perfusion is borderline or relapsing · oxygen requirement is climbing · the source is not controlled and re-intervention is likely · blood cultures remain positive · antibiotics are still being broadened · or renal function is deteriorating fast enough to need dose changes every few hours. A premature downgrade simply bounces the patient back, and bounce-backs do worse than patients who stayed.
ICU disposition beyond the floor. For a patient who cannot be weaned — prolonged ventilation, extensive wounds needing weeks of dressing changes, or multi-week parenteral therapy with ongoing instability — consider LTAC. And for recurrent severe infection in advanced irreversible illness, an honest goals-of-care conversation belongs in the plan: antibiotics can be a comfort measure or a burden, and which one they are depends entirely on what the patient wants.

Sources, trials & credits

This is a study reference, not a prescribing authority. Doses are for adults with normal renal and hepatic function unless stated. Always check your own institution's antibiogram and dosing guideline — local resistance patterns override every national figure here — and confirm doses against a current formulary before prescribing.

Key trials

TrialYearResultWhy it matters
MERINO2018ESBL bloodstream infection: 30-day mortality 12.3% pip-tazo vs 3.7% meropenem; failed non-inferiorityKilled the idea that pip-tazo is adequate for ESBL bacteraemia. Use a carbapenem.
STOP-IT2015N=518; a fixed 4-day course after adequate source control matched treating until physiologic normalisationEstablished short-course therapy for intra-abdominal infection — and that source control, not duration, is what cures it.
OVIVA2019N=1,054 bone/joint infection: failure at 1 year 13.2% oral vs 14.6% IV; catheter complications 1.0% vs 9.4%Ended the automatic "6 weeks of IV" reflex. The line is often riskier than the drug.
POET2019N=400 stabilised left-sided endocarditis: composite 9.0% partial-oral vs 12.1% IV; post-randomisation stay 3 vs 19 daysPartial oral therapy is possible in highly selected, stabilised endocarditis — an ID decision, not a floor decision.
SABATO2024Low-risk S. aureus bacteraemia: oral switch non-inferior (13% vs 12%) — but only 4.2% of screened patients were eligibleThe eligibility figure is the real lesson: almost no SAB patient qualifies.
Yahav · BALANCE2019 · 2025Uncomplicated gram-negative bacteraemia: 7 days non-inferior to 14. BALANCE N=3,608, 90-day mortality 14.5% vs 16.1%Seven days is the answer for stable, source-controlled gram-negative bacteraemia. Excludes S. aureus.
PTC (Dinh)2021CAP stable at day 3: 3 days of β-lactam non-inferior to 8 (cure 77% vs 68%)Pushes CAP duration below the 5-day guideline floor in stable patients.
Talan · Daum2016 · 2017After I&D of a cutaneous abscess, TMP-SMX improved cure (80.5% vs 73.6%); clindamycin and TMP-SMX both beat placebo for small abscessesChanged abscess practice — drainage plus an oral antibiotic, not drainage alone.
ProHOSP2009PCT-guided therapy in LRTI: antibiotic exposure 5.7 vs 8.7 days, adverse effects 19.8% vs 28.1%, non-inferior outcomesThe trial that made procalcitonin credible.
ProACT2018N=1,656, 14 US hospitals: no difference in antibiotic-days (4.2 vs 4.3)The essential counterweight — PCT only removes excess duration, and only if clinicians act on it.
SAPS · PRORATA2016 · 2010ICU PCT algorithms: SAPS median duration 5 vs 7 days with lower 28-day mortality (20% vs 25%); PRORATA gained 2.7 antibiotic-free daysSupports the "<0.5 ng/mL or ≥80% drop from peak" stopping rule in the ICU.
ACORN2023Vancomycin + pip-tazo vs vancomycin + cefepime: no difference in AKI; cefepime had more neurological dysfunctionOverturned a practice-changing observational signal. A lesson in evidence quality.
CAPE-COD2023Hydrocortisone in severe CAP reduced 28-day mortalitySteroids now belong in the severe-CAP conversation.
de Gans2002Dexamethasone before/with the first antibiotic dose reduced unfavourable outcome and mortality in bacterial meningitisWhy steroids must precede antibiotics — the benefit is blunting the inflammatory burst from bacterial lysis.
PEN-FAST · PALACE2020 · 2023PEN-FAST <3 has a 96.3% NPV; PALACE showed direct oral challenge non-inferior to skin testing in those patientsTurns penicillin-allergy delabelling into something any clinician can start.
Parente2018MRSA nasal PCR for MRSA pneumonia: NPV 96.5% overall, 98.1% in CAPThe single easiest vancomycin de-escalation available on the wards.
Hepburn2004Uncomplicated cellulitis: 5 days non-inferior to 10 in patients improving at day 5Halved cellulitis courses.
AVOD · DIABOLO2012 · 2017Uncomplicated acute diverticulitis: antibiotics did not accelerate recovery or prevent complicationsMade observation without antibiotics a legitimate option in mild disease.
Kumar2006In septic shock, each hour of delay to effective antimicrobial therapy after hypotension onset was associated with a measurable fall in survivalThe origin of the one-hour antibiotic target in septic shock.
Halm1998Once clinical stability is reached, subsequent deterioration requiring escalation occurs in ≤1%The evidence base for the discharge vital-sign criteria.
MASCC (Klastersky)2000Score ≥21 identifies low-risk febrile neutropenia (PPV 91%)The basis for outpatient oral management of selected febrile neutropenia.
CURB-65 (Lim)2003A five-item bedside score stratifying 30-day pneumonia mortalityThe simplest CAP disposition tool; ATS/IDSA prefer PSI/PORT for the admit decision.

Calculators linked out (not reimplemented here)

  • PSI / PORT Score — a 20-variable weighted model with a Step-1 algorithm for Class I; not reliably reproducible as a simple point total.
  • CISNE — better than MASCC for seemingly stable solid-tumour outpatients.
  • SOFA · LRINEC — note that a low LRINEC does not exclude necrotising infection.

All images are real photographs, micrographs, radiographs or human-drawn diagrams from Wikimedia Commons under CC0, public-domain, CC BY or CC BY-SA licences. No AI-generated medical imagery is used anywhere in this guide.

  • Image: How do different antibiotics work?.png — Our World in Data - Saloni Dattani (adapted from Sanseverino et al. 2018; Hutchings, Truman and Wilkinson 2019; icons from NIH BioArt), CC BY 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons) — Teaching overview mapping each antibiotic class to the bacterial target it attacks - cell wall synthesis, cell membrane, folate synthesis, DNA gyrase, RNA synthesis and protein synthesis.
  • Image: Chemical Structure of Penicillin.png — SM Smith96, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons) — Chemical structure of penicillin G: the strained four-membered beta-lactam ring (lower left, C=O plus ring N) fused to a thiazolidine ring - the pharmacophore shared by penicillins, cephalosporins and carbapenems.
  • Image: Site of cleavage by beta-lactamase.jpg — UIC College of Pharmacy, Public domain (Wikimedia Commons) — Beta-lactamase resistance: the enzyme hydrolyses the amide bond of the beta-lactam ring (arrow), opening it and inactivating the drug - the rationale for inhibitors such as tazobactam and for carbapenems (left).
  • Image: Streptococcal hemolysis.jpg — Y tambe, CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons) — Hemolysis patterns on sheep blood agar, streaked as the Greek letters: alpha (partial, green - S. mitis / viridans), beta (complete, clear - S. pyogenes) and gamma (no hemolysis - S. salivarius).
  • Image: Left cellulitis of leg.jpg — Stephen Ewen, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons) — Non-purulent cellulitis of the leg with the erythema margin outlined in pen and time-stamped - the bedside way to separate true antibiotic failure from expected early spread over the first 24-48 hours.
  • Image: X-ray of lobar pneumonia.jpg — Mikael Haggstrom, M.D., CC0 (Wikimedia Commons) — Chest radiograph showing right middle lobe consolidation silhouetting the right heart border - lobar community-acquired pneumonia, the imaging finding that anchors empiric CAP antibiotic choice.
  • Image: Antibiotic suceptible bacteria.jpg — Microrao, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons) — Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion on Mueller-Hinton agar: wide clear zones of inhibition around every antibiotic disk mark a fully susceptible isolate - zone diameter is measured in mm and read against CLSI breakpoints.
  • Image: Antibiotic resistant bacteria.jpg — Microrao, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons) — The same disk diffusion test on a resistant isolate: the bacterial lawn grows right up to nearly every disk (no zone), with only one small zone left - the visual signature of a multidrug-resistant organism.
  • Image: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase.jpg — Microrao, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons) — ESBL confirmatory disk test: the zone around ceftazidime plus clavulanic acid (CAC 30/10, right) is more than 5 mm larger than around ceftazidime alone (CAZ 30, left) - clavulanate restores activity, confirming an ESBL producer.
  • Image: Etest Vancomycin S aureus.jpg — Microrao, JJMMC, Davangere, Karnataka, India, Public domain (Wikimedia Commons) — Gradient MIC strip (Etest) for vancomycin: the teardrop-shaped ellipse of inhibition intersects the printed concentration scale at the MIC - here about 2 mcg/mL, the value compared against the susceptibility breakpoint.
  • Image: Streptococcus pneumoniae tested with Cefotaxime.jpg — Nathan Reading (Flickr), CC BY 2.0 (Wikimedia Commons) — Cefotaxime (CTX) gradient MIC strip on chocolate agar seeded with Streptococcus pneumoniae; the strip carries a 256 to 0.015 mcg/mL gradient and the edge of the elliptical inhibition zone reads out the MIC directly.
  • Image: E choli Gram.JPG — Bobjgalindo, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons) — Gram stain of Escherichia coli from a urinary tract infection: pink-red gram-negative rods (bacilli), the morphology that prompts gram-negative coverage for urinary, biliary and intra-abdominal sources.
  • Image: Gram positive cocci in clusters.jpg — Microrao, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons) — Gram stain showing gram-positive cocci in grape-like clusters - the classic morphology of Staphylococcus, which drives empiric anti-staphylococcal (and MRSA) coverage.
  • Image: Pus in Gram stain showing Gram positive cocci in singles, pairs and clusters.jpg — Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons) — Purulent specimen Gram stain: sheets of neutrophils with dark purple gram-positive cocci in clusters, several of them intracellular - evidence of true staphylococcal infection rather than contamination.
  • Image: Gram stain of Streptococcus pneumoniae.jpg — Arnold Kaufman, CC0 (Wikimedia Commons) — Gram stain of Streptococcus pneumoniae: gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci in pairs and short chains - the pathogen behind classic lobar community-acquired pneumonia and pneumococcal meningitis.
  • Image: MRSA on Brilliance MRSA Chromogenic Agar.jpg — Nathan Reading (Flickr), CC BY 2.0 (Wikimedia Commons) — Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus on selective chromogenic agar - MRSA forms distinctive denim-blue colonies, allowing isolation and de-escalation decisions before full susceptibilities return.
  • Image: Peptidoglycan-simple.png — Bradleyhintze, CC0 (Wikimedia Commons) — Peptidoglycan mesh: alternating N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid sugar backbones tied together by amino-acid cross-links - the rigid cell-wall lattice that beta-lactams and vancomycin target.
  • Image: Pseudomonas aeruginosa pigment production.jpg — HansN., CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons) — Pseudomonas aeruginosa panel: colony morphology plus the diffusible blue-green pyocyanin and yellow-green pyoverdin pigments (panels C, E-G) and gram-negative rods on Gram stain (panel J).
  • Image: Simple transpeptidase machanism cartoon.png — Bradleyhintze, CC0 (Wikimedia Commons) — Transpeptidase (penicillin-binding protein) cross-linking two peptidoglycan strands - the exact reaction beta-lactams block by acylating the enzyme active site, leaving an unstable wall and osmotic lysis.
